lectures.name: Intro to Diabetes
lectures.title: Type 1 vs Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
lectures.framing: Both types are diagnosed by the same glucose thresholds — what separates them is the mechanism producing the hyperglycemia: absolute autoimmune insulin deficiency in type 1 vs. a spectrum of insulin resistance and relative deficiency in type 2. The lecture takes type 1 first, then the diagnostic cut-offs, then type 2 and its eight defects.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ the alpha cells are spared in T1DM — the lesion is beta-cell specific. Autoantibody count, not presence, is what carries risk (1 = background risk, 3 = 40% in five years). Glutamic acid decarboxylase is the specific marker. Monozygotic concordance is higher in T2DM (90%) than T1DM (50%) — the counterintuitive fact worth remembering. And the octet explains why T2DM needs combination therapy: each drug class corrects a different defect.

blocks.html: 1. Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM): the mechanism

• Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) = immune-mediated destruction of islet beta cells → absolute insulin deficiency
    • glucagon-producing alpha cells are SPARED
  • Consequence of ↓ insulin
    • ① glucose cannot be used → stays in blood
    • ② body senses "starvation" → glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis release more glucose
  • Genetics
    • mostly polygenic; genes both within and outside the major histocompatibility complex
    • risk with family: 50% monozygotic twin · 5% non-identical sibling · 0.4% no family history
2. Autoantibodies in type 1

• Present in up to 85%
    • insulin/proinsulin (often appears after starting exogenous insulin)
    • glutamic acid decarboxylase — most specific marker, in 70%
    • insulinoma-associated protein 2 · zinc transporter 8
  • Risk depends on the count, not the presence
    • 1 antibody alone does NOT ↑ risk above baseline (~0.4%); 2 = 25% in 5 years, 3 = 40%
3. Diagnosing prediabetes and diabetes
• The same thresholds for both types; prediabetes is the grey zone between normal and diabetes.

• Fasting = no caloric intake for at least 8 hours · random = any time of day, regardless of the last meal
  • HbA1c is not used to diagnose suspected type 1 diabetes
4. Stages of type 1 diabetes

• Staged, all with beta-cell autoimmunity: the number of working beta cells falls across the stages
    • Stage 1 normoglycemia, pre-symptomatic
    • Stage 2 dysglycemia, pre-symptomatic
    • Stage 3 dysglycemia, symptomatic
    • e.g. a child with anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase + anti-insulin antibodies and a fasting glucose of 6.5 mmol/L = stage 2

blocks.alt: type 1 diabetes stages - beta-cell mass over time.png
blocks.cap: Stages 1 to 3 of type 1 diabetes: functional beta-cell mass falls long before symptoms appear

blocks.html: 5. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM)

• Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) = a spectrum: predominant insulin resistance with relative deficiency ↔ predominant secretory defect with resistance
    • no autoimmunity · no autoantibodies
    • indolent prodrome of dysglycemia lasting years
    • parallels the obesity epidemic (1980 → 2045: 108 million → 700 million)
  • Genetics: mostly polygenic
    • 90% monozygotic twin · 40% have an affected parent · 5–10% ↑ lifetime risk with a 1st-degree relative

rows: Same net hyperglycemia, produced by the eight defects below

blocks.html: 6. The "Ominous Octet"
• The "Ominous Octet" — eight defects driving T2DM hyperglycemia. Each is a drug target, which is why it is worth memorising in this direction.

blocks.alt: ominous octet - eight defects of type 2 diabetes (slide).png
blocks.cap: The ominous octet: eight organ defects that converge on hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes

rows: 80% of beta-cell function lost by the prediabetes range
↓ glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) + liver more sensitive to glucagon → ↑ gluconeogenesis
GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors
incretins normally act on hypothalamus + mesolimbic reward system to promote satiety
GLP-1RAs — why semaglutide causes weight loss
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) mRNA expression is itself ↑ by hyperglycemia → potentiates it
<mark class="lo">Insulin resistance, worsened by ↑ free fatty acids in muscle</mark>

Fat resistant to insulin's anti-lipolytic effect → ↑ free fatty acids stimulate gluconeogenesis and ↓ insulin secretion; once storage capacity is exceeded fat "spills" into muscle, liver and beta cells
Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) levels ↑ but insulin response to GIP is ↓; GLP-1 levels ↓

blocks.cap: Incretin actions: what GIP and GLP-1 do in the pancreas, brain, gut, fat, bone and heart

lectures.name: Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes
lectures.title: Approach to New-Onset Type 1 Diabetes
lectures.framing: The whole diagnosis turns on one question: are symptoms present? If yes, a single abnormal glucose is sufficient — do not delay treatment for a confirmatory test. The lecture runs symptoms → diagnosis → the four education pillars → why control matters → hypoglycemia.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ symptoms present → one abnormal glucose diagnoses diabetes; no symptoms → two are needed. The Diabetes Control and Complications Trial logic underlies everything here — intensive insulin therapy ↓ A1c and ↓ long-term microvascular complications but ↑ hypoglycemia, a trade-off now partly offset by pumps and continuous glucose monitors. Glucose gel works through buccal mucosa, so it can be given when swallowing is unsafe.

blocks.html: 1. Symptoms of new-onset diabetes

• History
    • three classic early symptoms nearly every patient has: polyuria (including nocturia / new bed-wetting), excessive thirst, weight loss despite unchanged appetite
    • then screen for late/severe features: vomiting · abdominal pain · dehydration · hypovolemic shock · hyperventilation (acidosis) · drowsiness · coma
  • Physical exam: hydration status · weight loss · level of consciousness · Kussmaul breathing · acetone breath

blocks.alt: type 1 diabetes - lack of insulin pathway to symptoms and ketoacidosis.png
blocks.cap: Lack of insulin: high glucose causes thirst and frequent urination, fat and protein breakdown cause weight loss, and ketone build-up causes acidosis, fast breathing and nausea

blocks.html: 2. Diagnosis
• Symptoms present → one abnormal glucose is enough; no symptoms → two abnormal measurements are needed

rows: ≥ 11.1 mmol/L ← the one that matters acutely

blocks.html: • HbA1c is not one of the type 1 diagnostic criteria — the deck lists only random (with symptoms), fasting and 2-hour glucose

• Investigations
    • random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 · urine dipstick for glucose and ketones (glycosuria + ketonuria)
    • serum C-peptide (is she making any insulin?)
    • arterial blood gas if diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is suspected
    • ⚠ fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and glycated hemoglobin (A1c) are usually unnecessary here — the diagnosis is already clear

blocks.html: 3. Management: the four education pillars

• Management — the four education pillars, delivered by a multidisciplinary team: dietician · social worker · diabetes nurse educator
  • Treatment: insulin + structured education · treat DKA emergently if present

rows:
4× per day (before meals + bedtime) · every 2–3 hours during illness · occasional nocturnal values · whenever hypoglycemic symptoms occur
Method: fingerprick meter or continuous glucose monitor

< 18 years, type 1 diabetes: FPG 4–8, post-prandial 5–10, A1c < 7.5%
Non-diabetic: FPG 3–6, A1c 4–6%
Severe/excessive hypoglycemia or hypoglycemia unawareness → pre-prandial target 6–10 mmol/L and a higher A1c

Bolus (short/rapid-acting) + basal (intermediate/long-acting); sliding scale dosed to blood glucose and carbohydrate load
3 injections/day = NPH + fast-acting · 4 injections/day = long-acting (glargine/detemir/degludec) + fast-acting · or a pump
Carbohydrate counting to match bolus dosing

Pumps (continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion, basal + bolus): better control, more reliable absorption, precise dosing, ↓ hypoglycemia risk, ↓ long-term complications, flexibility with food, shift work and time zones
Continuous glucose monitor: interstitial glucose every 5 minutes · alerts when out of range or expected to be within 20 minutes
Time in range = 3.9–10 mmol/L: the same A1c of 7% can hide 19% or 71% time in range

blocks.alt: basal-bolus insulin concept - mimicking the normal pancreas.png
blocks.cap: Basal-bolus insulin copies the normal pancreas: a mealtime bolus at breakfast, lunch and supper, plus a steady basal dose given at bedtime

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • Adjusting multiple daily injection doses: fix the insulin given BEFORE the abnormal reading — low at lunch → ↓ breakfast rapid-acting · high at bedtime → ↑ supper rapid-acting
• Follow-up: annual urinalysis for albuminuria (diabetic nephropathy screening)
4. Why control matters: the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial

• Intensive insulin therapy ↓ A1c and ↓ long-term microvascular complications but ↑ hypoglycemia
    • A1c held at ~7% intensive vs ~9% conventional over ~9 years
    • the trade-off is now partly offset by pumps and continuous glucose monitors
5. Acute complication: hypoglycemia
• Hypoglycemia symptoms come in two waves, and the order is the point

• Treatment
    • give ~15 g of fast-acting sugar
    • glucose tablet or juice · glucose gel (absorbed rapidly across buccal mucosa) · glucagon (intramuscular, subcutaneous or intranasal) · intravenous dextrose
  • Prevention: treat early symptoms promptly · monitor regularly · adjust insulin before and after exercise · adhere to the meal plan

lectures.name: Pharmacology of Insulin
lectures.title: Insulin Preparations
lectures.framing: Choose a preparation based on what the insulin is covering — a meal (bolus) or the fasting state (basal). Every preparation works the same way once it reaches the receptor; they differ only in how fast they get there. The lecture runs structure → uses → the preparations → mechanism → adverse effects → practical points.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Analogues are NOT more effective at lowering HbA1c than human insulin — they are safer and more convenient (faster onset, better postprandial match, lower variability, less early-night hypoglycemia). Only regular insulin can be given intravenously. Basal insulins must never be used in pumps, and most basal insulins must not be mixed with another insulin before injection. Insulin does not interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other drugs — but drugs that alter glucose metabolism (e.g. steroids ↑ hepatic glucose production) change how well it works. Exogenous insulin is imperfect because physiological secretion is glucose-dependent, and that fine-tuning is lost.

blocks.html: 1. Structure sets the kinetics

• Insulin = two peptide chains (A and B) linked by disulphide bridges · made by beta cells as preproinsulin → proinsulin → insulin + C-peptide
    • molecules pair into dimers and then hexamers (a trimer of dimers) · insulin binds its receptor only as a monomer
  • Onset and duration are set by one thing: how fast monomers dissociate from the hexamer
    • anything that stabilizes the hexamer (zinc, protamine, self-aggregation, albumin binding) → slower onset, longer duration
    • bolus insulins are built to release monomers faster · basal insulins to release them slower

blocks.html: 2. Clinical uses
• Diabetes · hyperkalemia · hyperglycemic crisis (diabetic ketoacidosis) · diagnostic testing
3. The preparations

• Rapid analogues vs regular human insulin
    • faster onset (5–15 min vs 30–60 min) · better match to the post-meal surge · lower variability → less early-night hypoglycemia, fewer bedtime snacks
    • Analogues are NOT more effective at lowering glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) than human insulin — they are safer and more convenient

blocks.html: 4. Mechanism of action

• Identical for every preparation once the active monomer is reached
    • insulin receptor activation → ↑ translocation of GLUT-4 to the membrane (glucose uptake) · ↑ glycogen synthase · ↑ lipogenesis · ↑ cell growth/division
    • preparations differ only in pharmacokinetics, never in mechanism
  • Overall actions: ↑ glycogen, fatty acid and protein synthesis · ↑ leptin · ↓ gluconeogenesis · ↓ hunger
  • Why exogenous insulin is imperfect: physiological secretion is glucose-dependent, and that fine-tuning is lost
5. Adverse effects

rows: Makes absorption slow and unpredictable → rotate sites systematically
Usually to the additives, not the insulin

blocks.html:
• Causes of hypoglycemia
    • missed meal or unusual exercise · excess basal when prandial was what was needed · no dose adjustment for activity
    • loss of renal function (↓ clearance) · cognitive impairment or unfamiliar device · interacting drugs (e.g. steroids)
6. Therapeutic considerations

• Route: only regular insulin can be given intravenously
  • Pumps: basal insulins must never be used in pumps · glulisine clots pumps more often
  • Mixing: most basal insulins must not be mixed with another insulin before injection
  • Factors affecting absorption
    • route · formulation · dose · injection site · local blood flow (massage, hot tubs) · muscle activity (exercise)
  • Interactions
    • insulin does not interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other drugs
    • but drugs that alter glucose metabolism (e.g. steroids ↑ hepatic glucose production) change how well it works

lectures.name: Clinically Useful Endocrine Principles
lectures.title: Approach to a Suspected Endocrine Problem
lectures.framing: Every endocrine problem sorts into one of two kinds: structural (a mass) or functional (too much or too little hormone) — and both can be present at once. The sorting question determines the entire workup. The lecture orients you to hormones, sorts the problem, then works through masses, hormone problems and the dynamic tests.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ the suppression/stimulation pairing is the single most testable idea here — excess is tested by trying to turn it off, deficiency by trying to turn it on. Primary adrenal insufficiency loses both cortisol AND aldosterone, which is what separates it from central causes. A benign mass can still be clinically important through pure mass effect. And always ask whether an exogenous hormone explains the picture before working up the gland.

blocks.html: 1. Hormones: what they do and how they reach their target

• Four jobs
    • reproduction (estradiol, testosterone, prolactin)
    • growth and development (growth hormone, sex steroids)
    • maintaining the internal environment (triiodothyronine, antidiuretic hormone, parathyroid hormone)
    • making, storing and using energy (insulin, glucagon, cortisol)
  • By distance to target: autocrine = the cell itself · paracrine = a nearby cell · endocrine = distant, reached via the bloodstream
2. Structural or functional? The sorting question

blocks.alt: endocrine gland problem - structure vs function and what to do - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Sorting tree for an endocrine gland problem: structure (benign or malignant) versus function (hyper- or hypofunction), with the management each branch leads to

blocks.html: 3. Structural problems: a mass

• Two questions
    • benign or malignant?
    • does the enlargement itself cause clinical effects? a benign mass can still be clinically important through pure mass effect
  • Mass effect: pituitary → optic chiasm, cranial nerves III/IV/VI, trigeminal V1/V2 · thyroid → dysphagia

rows: Metastases to the adrenal · malignant pheochromocytoma · adrenal cortical carcinoma

Focal enlargement = nodules
papillary thyroid carcinoma · follicular thyroid carcinoma · medullary thyroid carcinoma

Diffuse enlargement = goiters
Graves disease · Hashimoto's thyroiditis · iodine deficiency · toxic multinodular goiter

blocks.html: 4. Functional problems: too much or too little hormone

• Four questions to ask of any functional problem
    • What does the hormone do?
    • What feedback loops could be affected?
    • Is the problem in the gland itself (primary) or somewhere else (secondary / tertiary / central)?
    • Can this be explained by an exogenous source of hormone? — ask this before working up the gland

rows:
primary adrenal insufficiency (cortisol AND aldosterone deficiency)
congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency)

Hyperthyroidism / thyrotoxicosis
Graves disease · iatrogenic (oral thyroxine) · thyroiditis (hyper stage) · gestational thyrotoxicosis · thyroid-stimulating hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma

5. Dynamic testing
• The logic is always the mirror of the problem. Suspect excess → suppress. Suspect deficiency → stimulate.

rows: <mark class="lo">Stimulate a failing gland and watch it fail to respond</mark>
Oral glucose normally suppresses growth hormone
Arginine-growth hormone-releasing hormone stimulation test, or insulin tolerance test
Saline infusion, or 3-day oral sodium loading

lectures.name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology
lectures.title: Diagnosing Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and the Grey Zone
lectures.framing: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) and T2DM share identical diagnostic thresholds — so the diagnostic work is (1) crossing the threshold, (2) deciding how many measurements you need, and (3) working out which type you are looking at. The lecture then turns to what else comes with T2DM, why it happens, who gets it, and how common it is.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ the thresholds mark where retinopathy risk rises, not cardiovascular risk. Symptomatic → one measurement; asymptomatic → two. Do not diagnose during acute illness (myocardial infarction, sepsis, steroids) — suspect, then confirm on recovery. C-peptide and anti-GAD move in opposite directions between the two types: low C-peptide + high anti-GAD = T1DM. >90% of all diabetes is Type 2; 589 million adults live with diabetes worldwide (~1 in 9), ~43% of them undiagnosed, and ~30% of Canadians have diabetes or prediabetes. Finally — a T2DM diagnosis is not necessarily permanent: weight loss, activity and diet can return glucose below the diabetic range, though it can recur, so keep re-checking periodically.

blocks.html: 1. Diagnostic criteria and the grey zone

• How many measurements
    • symptomatic → one measurement; asymptomatic → two. · a repeat confirmatory test is done on another day
    • do not diagnose during acute illness (myocardial infarction, sepsis, steroids) — suspect, then confirm on recovery

• Why these particular numbers? The cut-points were not chosen arbitrarily and they are not the level at which cardiovascular risk rises
    • they mark the glycemic level at which the risk of diabetic retinopathy rises sharply

blocks.alt: retinopathy prevalence by glucose and a1c - why the diagnostic thresholds.png
blocks.cap: Retinopathy prevalence stays flat across glucose and A1c levels, then jumps at the diabetic cut-points

blocks.html: • ⚠ The grey zone is the target population for T2DM prevention — see 12 - Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes
2. Telling type 1 from type 2

rows: Indolent prodrome (impaired fasting glucose / impaired glucose tolerance) lasting years
Often needed; results vary with physical stress, weight, activity
Sudden dramatic weight loss → severe hyperglycemia, incipient T1DM
Recent weight gain, or being very active then suddenly stopping (lack of muscle work tips glucose into diabetic range)

blocks.html: • ⚠ These tests are often unnecessary — usually time and the response to medications reveal the type.

blocks.html: 3. More than hyperglycemia: non-glycemic features and metabolic syndrome

• T2DM is not only a disease of hyperglycemia
    • abnormal lipids (hypertriglyceridemia, low high-density lipoprotein, small dense low-density lipoprotein)
    • ↑ systemic and vascular inflammation · ↑ free fatty acids · hypertension · sleep apnea

cols: metabolic syndrome — some or all of
rows: essential hypertension · low high-density lipoprotein · hypertriglyceridemia · ↑ waist-to-hip ratio (visceral fat) · dysglycemia or T2DM
Flags ↑ risk of cardiovascular disease and T2DM. In a patient who already has T2DM, metabolic syndrome raises cardiovascular risk further still

blocks.html: 4. Pathophysiology: insulin resistance and insulin deficiency
• Two problems, and by diagnosis both are present

rows: Needs more insulin than normal to move glucose into liver, adipose and skeletal muscle

Not enough insulin for the body's needs
T1DM = absolute · T2DM = relative
Genetics · high fat / refined carb diet · lack of muscle activity · excess adipose tissue and fatty liver · systemic inflammation (adipocytokines) · abnormal mitochondria
Genetics · surgery (pancreatectomy) · excess glucose (glucose toxicity feedback loop) · excess free fatty acids from visceral fat lipolysis
resistance → ↑ demand on pancreas → pancreas cannot keep up → diabetic glucose
deficiency → glucose rises → glucose toxicity → further pancreatic stress → diabetic glucose

blocks.alt: natural history of type 2 diabetes - insulin resistance, production and glucose.png
blocks.cap: Natural history of type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance rises early, insulin production compensates then fails, and glucose climbs

blocks.html: 5. Risk factors

• Genetic: mostly polygenic
    • 90% monozygotic twin concordance · 40% have an affected parent · 5–10% ↑ lifetime risk with a 1st-degree relative
  • Environmental: obesogenic foods (low fibre, high fat, high refined sugars) · "portion creep" · inactivity · obesity · lower socio-economic status
  • Intrauterine: birth-weight extremes (both under- and overweight) · in-utero exposure to high glucose · prematurity
  • Populations at particular risk: Asian, South Asian, Hispanic, Indigenous, African American / African-descent, and women with previous gestational diabetes
6. Prevalence

• >90% of all diabetes is Type 2; 589 million adults live with diabetes worldwide (~1 in 9)
    • ~43% of them undiagnosed
    • ~30% of Canadians have diabetes or prediabetes
7. Lowering blood glucose: the diagnosis is not always permanent

• A T2DM diagnosis is not necessarily permanent: weight loss, activity and diet can return glucose below the diabetic range
    • it can recur, so keep re-checking glucose / A1c periodically
  • But not always reversible: with significant insulin deficiency, glucose stays high despite excellent lifestyle change — not all T2DM is due to being overweight and underactive

lectures.name: Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes
lectures.title: Complications of Diabetes
lectures.framing: The acute emergencies separate on one variable: is there enough insulin to suppress lipolysis? Enough → no ketones → hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS). Not enough → ketogenesis → diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). The lecture covers the two emergencies, their treatment and prevention, then the chronic small- and large-vessel complications and why they happen.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ abdominal pain and vomiting = DKA, not HHS. Hours = DKA, days = HHS. T1DM = DKA, older T2DM = HHS. SGLT2 inhibitors can precipitate DKA — and appear again in the sick-day rules as a drug to stop. Potassium falls with treatment, not before it. Proprioception goes early in peripheral neuropathy, and feet are affected before hands because of nerve length.

blocks.html: 1. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)

• Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) = no insulin at all → unopposed lipolysis → ketone production → anion gap metabolic acidosis
  • Causes: absolute insulin deficiency → type 1 diabetes (T1DM)
    • illness — anything ① dehydrating or ② physically stressful (gastroenteritis, myocardial infarction, stroke, sepsis, pancreatitis)
    • lack of insulin — 1st diagnosis of T1DM, forgetting / withholding / rationing insulin, insulin pump malfunction
    • medications — steroids, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, cocaine
  • Presents as: ⏰ evolves over HOURS
    • polyuria · polydipsia · weight loss · nausea, VOMITING, ABDOMINAL PAIN
    • progresses to lethargy and coma if untreated
  • Physical exam: toxic appearance · hypotension + tachycardia (shock) · dehydration (dry membranes, poor skin turgor) · acetone smell on breath · Kussmal's breathing
  • Investigations
    • ↑ blood glucose (often > 15) · ↑ serum and urine ketones
    • ↑ anion gap — follow it during treatment · ↓ serum pH (acidosis) · ↓ serum bicarbonate (consumed; pH may be ~7.0) · plasma osmolality mildly ↑
    • Na⁺ ↑ or ↓ — high sugars falsely lower Na⁺, so correct for glucose
    • K⁺ normal or ↓ — total body K⁺ is depleted even when serum looks normal
    • ↑ creatinine (dehydration)
2. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)

• Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) = enough insulin to inhibit adipose breakdown into ketones, but not enough to prevent hyperglycemia → profound hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality without significant acidosis
  • Causes: relative insulin deficiency → type 2 diabetes (T2DM), usually older patients
    • illness — dehydrating or physically stressful · lack of insulin — rationing, missed doses · drug effects — steroids worsen insulin resistance
  • Presents as: ⏰ evolves over DAYS
    • polyuria · polydipsia · lethargy → obtundation (rarely coma)
    • NO abdominal pain and NO vomiting
  • Investigations: same panel, but the discriminating pattern is very high glucose · ↑↑ plasma osmolality · minimal or absent ketones · pH and serum bicarbonate near normal — no significant anion gap
  • The biochemical line between them — memorize this table.
3. Treating a hyperglycemic emergency

• Both require emergent treatment; fluid deficits are very large — even larger in HHS
    • ① ABCs — airway, breathing, circulation
    • ② Fluids — normal saline first, often many litres · add dextrose once glucose reaches ~12–14 mmol/L (5% dextrose in water with normal saline) so the insulin infusion can continue without causing hypoglycemia — normal glucose is not the immediate goal
    • ③ Insulin — ALWAYS required in DKA, almost always in HHS
    • ④ Monitoring every 1–2 hours — level of consciousness · Na⁺, K⁺, pH · glucose hourly on an insulin drip · volume status (especially elderly — watch for heart failure)
  • HHS: same protocol — these patients are older, so monitor volume status especially closely

blocks.title: The two traps that kill
blocks.html:
① Potassium. Total body K⁺ is depleted even when the initial serum potassium looks normal — in DKA, low insulin has driven K⁺ extracellularly. Once you give fluid and insulin, K⁺ shifts back intracellularly and falls sharply, causing arrhythmias and death. K⁺ replacement is often required during treatment.

② Glucose falling too fast. Intravenous fluids and insulin will drop glucose. Add dextrose to the fluids so insulin can keep running until the dehydration — and in DKA the acidosis — is corrected.
• Then look for the cause — both emergencies should spark a search for the precipitant
4. Prevention: sick-day rules

• Type 1: continue SOME insulin even when not eating (lower-dose basal) · monitor glucose and urine ketones frequently
  • Type 2: monitor glucose frequently
    • STOP dehydrating medications during gastrointestinal upset — SGLT2 inhibitors, diuretics, metformin
    • the stress of illness raises sugars, so taking some insulin is appropriate
  • Always ask why — common themes: withholding insulin to control weight (DKA) · withholding medication for financial reasons · uncertainty about sick-day rules · new medications, especially steroids · big body stresses (infection, myocardial infarction, stroke)
5. Chronic complications: microvascular vs macrovascular
• Never used to frighten patients into compliance — they can occur despite excellent self-management

rows: myocardial infarction · stroke · peripheral vascular disease
Capillary basement membrane thickening; matrix accumulation in the glomerulus → fibrosis → ↓ filtration surface
↑ free fatty acids → atherosclerosis → plaque in coronary and cranial arteries

blocks.html: 6. Diabetic retinopathy

• diabetic retinopathy — the most common microvascular complication
  • Staging — only the third stage threatens vision

rows: No — can even improve with good glycemic control
No, but at risk of progressing — monitor frequently
Retinal infarcts (cotton wool spots), lipid exudates, macular edema (can change vision)
New fragile vessels, risk of bleeding into the vitreous

blocks.alt: non-proliferative vs proliferative diabetic retinopathy (fundus drawings).png
blocks.cap: Non-proliferative retinopathy (aneurysms, hard exudates, hemorrhages) versus proliferative retinopathy (growth of abnormal vessels)

blocks.html: 7. Diabetic nephropathy

• diabetic nephropathy — #1 cause of renal failure in the USA
  • Nephropathy = proteinuria > 500 mg/24 h, preceded by microalbuminuria 30–299 mg/24 h
  • Treatment: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors / angiotensin receptor blockers — even in patients WITHOUT hypertension

blocks.alt: pathology of diabetic nephropathy.png
blocks.cap: Diabetic kidney disease in the glomerulus: thickened basement membrane, mesangial expansion, lost fenestrations and podocyte injury compared with a healthy glomerulus

blocks.html: 8. Diabetic neuropathy

• Peripheral sensorimotor — most common
    • "glove and stocking" · feet worse than hands because longer nerves conduct proportionally slower · proprioception lost early
    • risk of ulcers, infection, amputation, neuropathic arthropathy (Charcot foot)
  • Autonomic — gastroparesis (common in T1DM) · erectile dysfunction
  • Cranial — most commonly third nerve palsy · also Bell's palsy
  • Amyotrophy — wasting of large proximal muscles from lumbosacral plexus damage, most common in T2DM

blocks.alt: stocking and glove distribution.png
blocks.cap: Glove-and-stocking neuropathy: sensation fades first in the feet and lower legs, then the hands, because the longest nerves are affected first; ankle reflexes drop before knee reflexes

blocks.html: 9. Macrovascular and other complications

• Myocardial infarction · stroke — free fatty acid-driven plaque in coronary and cranial arteries
  • Peripheral vascular disease: always ask about intermittent claudication and check pulses in both legs — unchecked, it leads to amputation
  • Other: ↑ risk of cataracts and glaucoma
10. Why complications happen at all

• hyperglycemia is toxic to vessels and nerves · drives oxidative stress and free radicals · ↑ intracellular sorbitol → osmotic swelling · ↑ vascular endothelial growth factor → angiogenesis
  • Contributing: hypertension · cholesterol/atherosclerosis · protein glycation · inflammation and a hypercoagulable state driving thrombosis

lectures.title: Glucose-Lowering Drugs in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM)
lectures.framing: Choose an agent based on which step of glucose metabolism is being manipulated, then narrow by hypoglycemia risk, effect on weight, and organ function. The lecture takes the drug groups in turn — sensitizers, secretagogues, then drugs that change absorption or excretion — and ends on choosing a second-line agent.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ GLP-1RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors are the agents with proven cardiovascular benefit — pick one in a patient with CV disease. The incretin agents are secretagogues too, but only the glucose-independent secretagogues (SUs, meglitinides) carry meaningful hypoglycemia risk, because they release insulin independent of glucose level; the incretins do not, because their secretion is glucose-dependent. Weight gain: TZDs, SUs, meglitinides. Weight loss: GLP-1RAs, SGLT2 inhibitors, (metformin). Renal function matters twice: metformin is excreted unchanged in urine (lactic acidosis if it accumulates), and SGLT2 inhibitors lose efficacy as renal function falls.

• Therapeutic goals in T2DM: control symptoms · individualized glycemic control · avoid hypoglycemia · minimize acute and chronic complications · control associated risk factors

lectures.name: Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes
lectures.title: Glycemic Goals of Care
lectures.framing: The target is never a single number — it is a negotiation between preventing long-term complications and avoiding hypoglycemia now. Tight control buys microvascular benefit; severe hypoglycemia carries ↑ mortality. The lecture runs why targets matter → how glucose is measured → reading it from symptoms → setting the target.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ severity of hypoglycemia is defined by whether the patient can treat it themselves — not by the glucose number. A1c is the best-validated marker of control but lags, so it never replaces glucose readings when you are actively changing therapy. CGM measures interstitial, not blood, glucose. Tight control helps microvascular outcomes most; macrovascular benefit is probably yes in T1DM, probably not in T2DM.

blocks.html: 1. Why the target matters
• It changes both outcomes and your prescribing

rows: Symptomatic hyperglycemia · diabetic ketoacidosis / hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state · hypoglycemia

Microvascular — retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy
Macrovascular — stroke, myocardial infarction, peripheral vascular disease
A1c > 7% is associated with ↑ micro- and macrovascular risk; both fasting and post-prandial glucose correlate directly with complication risk
Tight control improves microvascular outcomes across multiple trials
Whether to start glucose-lowering drugs — and which (insulin, orals, or both) · doses and timing · intensity of monitoring (continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) vs. fingerstick)

blocks.html:
• Tight control helps microvascular outcomes most; macrovascular benefit: type 1 probably yes, type 2 probably not — the cardiovascular benefit of empagliflozin or liraglutide in type 2 is not clearly mediated by better glycemia
  • But tight control (A1c ~6.0%) ↑ severe hypoglycemia, which is linked to ↑ mortality — not ideal for older/frail patients, long diabetes duration, advanced coronary artery disease or prior severe hypoglycemia

• A1c is the best-validated marker of control but lags, so it never replaces glucose readings when you are actively changing therapy
  • How often to check depends on
    • type of diabetes — type 1 needs 4+/day, before each insulin dose, and often benefits from continuous glucose monitoring
    • type of therapy — sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia → check more
    • changes to therapy · adequacy of control · literacy and numeracy · propensity for and awareness of hypoglycemia · occupational requirements · acute illness

lectures.name: Introduction to Obesity
lectures.title: Obesity — Assessment and Management
lectures.framing: Obesity is a complex, progressive, relapsing chronic disease — abnormal or excessive body fat that impairs health. The lecture defines it, explains why it happens, then walks the 5 A's and the treatment ladder. BMI alone does not predict adiposity-related complications; stage the impact, not just the number.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The most serious post-bariatric deficiency is thiamine — give it before any glucose or you precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy. tirzepatide (dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide) beats semaglutide beats naltrexone-bupropion for weight loss. The BMI cut-off drops to 25 for South and East Asian patients. EOSS stages the functional impact, which is what determines bariatric referral — not BMI alone. Ghrelin is the only fasting/hunger hormone here; everything else in the list promotes satiety. The pharmacotherapy stopping rule is 5% at 12 weeks. Gastric banding is explicitly not recommended. And 20% of Canadians have obesity, with the socioeconomic gradient running opposite ways by sex — ↓ socioeconomic status means ↑ obesity in women, ↓ in men.

blocks.html: 1. Definition — thresholds are ethnicity-specific

• Obesity = BMI ≥ 30 (≥ 25 in South and East Asian patients), plus waist circumference (WC), because BMI alone is insufficient
  • South and East Asian: overweight = 23.0–24.9, obesity ≥ 25.0 kg/m²
  • Thresholds move because BMI and WC do not account for body frame, musculature, or propensity for visceral adiposity
• ⚠ South and East Asian individuals develop visceral adiposity and obesity-related disease at a lower BMI — this is why the cut-off moves
2. Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS)
• Stages the functional and health impact of obesity, not the body size — and it is what is used when referring to the bariatric program

blocks.alt: Edmonton Obesity Staging System.png
blocks.cap: Edmonton Obesity Staging System: stage 0 has no obesity-related problems, stage 2 an established comorbidity needing treatment, stage 4 severe end-stage disease; stage by health impact, not by body mass index

blocks.html: 3. Complications — the 4 M's

blocks.lead: Use this as the assessment checklist, not a list to memorise loosely.
rows: Cognition · depression · attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder · addiction · psychosis · eating disorders · trauma · insomnia
sleep apnea · osteoarthritis · chronic pain · gastroesophageal reflux disease · incontinence · venous thromboembolism · intertrigo · plantar fasciitis
type 2 diabetes (T2DM) · dyslipidemia · essential hypertension · gout · fatty liver · gallstones · polycystic ovarian syndrome · cancer
Education · employment · income · insurance · benefits · disability · weight loss programs · bariatric supplies

blocks.html: 4. Prevalence

• 20% of Canadians have obesity
  • Socioeconomic status runs opposite ways by sex: ↓ socioeconomic status means ↑ obesity in women, ↓ in men
5. Pathophysiology — far more than energy in vs. energy out

• Genetics: 60–70% of BMI is genetically determined.
  • Early-life events: maternal starvation in pregnancy predisposes offspring to obesity
    • intrauterine growth restriction → energy hoarding → later obesity
  • Other contributors: iatrogenic (steroids, antidepressants/antipsychotics) · gut microbiome and circadian rhythm (shift workers) · social determinants of health (food/income insecurity, housing instability) · environment and culture
  • Brain drivers of food-seeking
    • hypothalamus (homeostasis) · mesolimbic system (pleasure) · frontal lobe (executive control)
    • dopamine = wanting food, opioids = liking food
• Hormones of hunger and satiety

rows: ghrelin — made in the stomach, ↑ hunger and food intake

insulin, amylin — pancreas
glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP), cholecystokinin, peptide YY — intestines
leptin, adiponectin — adipose tissue

blocks.html: • After weight loss, these hormones shift to drive the return to the usual weight setpoint — why obesity relapses

blocks.alt: hunger and satiety hormones - ghrelin vs fed-state hormones - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Hunger and satiety hormones: ghrelin from the stomach in the fasting state, and insulin, amylin, peptide YY, GLP-1, cholecystokinin, leptin and adiponectin in the fed state, all acting on the hypothalamus

blocks.html: 6. Assessment — bias, stigma and the 5 A's

• Bias and stigma
    • 56% have attempted weight loss between 2 and 20 times — assume effort, not inaction
    • 95% of patients with severe obesity want to lose weight
    • chairs, exam tables, bathrooms and scales must accommodate the patient
    • place the scale in a private area, and do not announce weight unless they ask to hear it
  • ASK — ask permission to discuss weight
    • be non-judgemental · explore readiness for change · use motivational interviewing
  • ASSESS — stage the disease and find root causes
    • EOSS stage · BMI + WC if BMI ≥ 25 · the 4 M's
    • History: weight history · contributors · rule out hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome, medications, genetic disorders · cultural and family factors · diet and exercise history
    • Physical exam: BMI · WC · blood pressure · acanthosis, hirsutism, Cushingoid features
    • Labs: glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) · lipid panel · serum thyroid-stimulating hormone · alanine aminotransferase
  • ADVISE — risks, benefits, options
    • The goal is health and wellness, not a number.
    • first goal may simply be stabilising weight · behavioural change yields 3–5%
  • AGREE — realistic expectations and SMART goals (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound)
    • 0.5–1.0 kg (1–2 lb) per week; 5–10% total loss over 6–12 months
  • ASSIST — barriers, resources, follow-up
    • referrals (e.g. cardiology before an exercise plan) · contingency plans for travel · financial reality — dieticians are often out of pocket

rule out secondary causes"] D --> E["ADVISE: health and wellness, not a number"] E --> F["AGREE: SMART goals (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound)

blocks.html: 7. Management — two foundations

• Medical nutrition therapy — for all Canadians, regardless of body size
    • personalized · refer to a registered dietician, especially with celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease
  • Physical activity — for all
    • 30–60 min most days, moderate–vigorous + resistance training
    • small weight and fat loss, but improves cardiometabolic parameters and is key to maintaining loss
8. Management — three pillars

• Psychological, as appropriate
    • Behaviour modification · manage sleep, stress, time
    • cognitive behavioural therapy and/or acceptance and commitment therapy
  • Pharmacological — BMI ≥ 30, or ≥ 27 with complications
    • Efficacy order: tirzepatide (GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide) > semaglutide (GLP-1) > naltrexone-bupropion · orlistat rarely used
    • Should achieve ≥ 5% weight loss after 12 weeks at maximally tolerated dose — if not, change agent
    • adjunct to lifestyle, but likely lifelong
    • average placebo-subtracted weight loss: tirzepatide 20.9% · semaglutide 12.4% · naltrexone-bupropion 4.8% · orlistat 2.9%
    • GLP-1 agonists and tirzepatide: contraindicated in pregnancy and with a personal/family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) or medullary thyroid cancer (MTC)
  • Bariatric surgery — BMI ≥ 40, or ≥ 35 with complications, or ≥ 30 with poorly controlled T2DM
    • 25–30% weight loss; ↓ long-term mortality
    • procedures: sleeve gastrectomy · Roux-en-Y gastric bypass · biliopancreatic diversion ± duodenal switch · laparoscopic gastric banding no longer performed
    • After surgery: thiamine before glucose — always

blocks.cap: Bariatric procedures: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy, biliopancreatic diversion and laparoscopic gastric band

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Before bariatric surgery: smoking cessation is mandatory, and must be maintained after · limit alcohol + carbonated drinks · treat and manage mental health conditions first
  • Not a candidate: unstable psychiatric illness · untreated substance use · malignancy / ↓ life expectancy · cannot adhere to long-term follow-up
  • Post-operative deficiencies (worst after Roux-en-Y, biliopancreatic diversion): protein (commonest macronutrient) · iron, vitamin B12, calcium/vitamin D, thiamine, vitamin A

lectures.name: Prevention of Complications of Diabetes
lectures.title: Preventing the Complications of Diabetes
lectures.framing: Three numbers drive prevention — glycated hemoglobin (A1c), blood pressure, and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) — and each has its own first-line drug and its own set of complications it prevents. Glycemic control alone is not enough: it barely moves macrovascular risk.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Glycemic control prevents microvascular disease; blood pressure control is what prevents macrovascular disease in T2DM. ACEi/ARB are given for nephropathy even in patients without hypertension (see 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes). Feet are examined daily at home and at every clinic visit — the monofilament test detects the loss of protective sensation before ulceration. The > 15 years of diabetes clause matters: a 35-year-old diagnosed at 18 qualifies for a statin.

blocks.html: 1. What the trials showed

• The two trials: Diabetes Control and Complications Trial 1993 for type 1 diabetes (T1DM) · UK Prospective Diabetes Study 1998 for type 2 diabetes (T2DM)
  • Better glycemic control and more intensive regimens produced
    • microvascular complications: ✅ ↓ risk of developing or worsening
    • macrovascular complications: NO effect from glycemic control — but ↓ blood pressure ↓ cardiovascular disease risk in T2DM
    • hypoglycemia: ↑ risk — the cost of intensive control

blocks.cap: Diabetes Control and Complications Trial design: 1441 people with type 1 diabetes, conventional versus intensive insulin for 6.5 years

blocks.alt: a1c vs retinopathy and severe hypoglycemia risk - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Risk of retinopathy against risk of severe hypoglycemia across glycated hemoglobin: the trade-off intensive control makes

blocks.html: 2. Lifestyle interventions

• Home monitoring of glucose AND blood pressure
  • Smoking cessation — ↓ risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral arterial disease, and possibly retinopathy
  • Activity + weight loss if ↑ BMI — ↓ blood pressure and blood glucose
  • Annual ophthalmology screening — for diabetic retinopathy
  • Examine feet DAILY for open wounds
    • if vision impaired — ask a family member, or refer to chiropody · ensure comfortable shoes
3. In-clinic monitoring — feet, blood pressure, LDL
• Foot exam, every visit — Inspect for calluses and ulcers · assess pedal pulses · monofilament exam

blocks.cap: Monofilament test: press until the filament buckles, at the sites that best detect loss of protective sensation

blocks.html: • The three targets

rows: ≤ 7% (see 08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes)
angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) (or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs))
Cardiovascular outcomes, renal impairment, and retinopathy

blocks.html: 4. Drugs that protect beyond glucose

• Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors (e.g. empagliflozin) → cardiovascular AND renal protection.
  • Incretin analogues (e.g. liraglutide) → cardiovascular protection.
  • Coronary artery disease prevention — the age and duration triggers are the testable part

rows:
> 30 years AND diabetes > 15 years → statin
≥ 40 years → statin

≥ 55 years AND another CAD risk factor (proteinuria, retinopathy, left ventricular hypertrophy) → ACEi or ARB IN ADDITION to a statin
renal disease → ACEi or ARB
ACEi or ARB — blood pressure target < 130/80

blocks.html: 5. At diagnosis — refer early, pick the first drug

• Refer early
    • dietician — dietary change to ↓ complication risk
    • diabetes nurse educator — sugar testing, what to do when low or sick
    • optometrist — yearly
  • First medication
    • Insulin — all T1DM, and T2DM patients who are very symptomatic (polydipsia, polyuria, yeast infections, weight loss, malaise)
    • metformin — T2DM without many symptoms and no liver or renal concerns

lectures.name: Pregnancy and Diabetes
lectures.title: Diabetes in Pregnancy
lectures.framing: The single discriminating question is when the hyperglycemia starts. Pre-existing diabetes mellitus (DM) is present during organogenesis (weeks 3–16) → congenital malformations. Gestational diabetes (GDM) appears at 24–28 weeks, after organogenesis → NO congenital malformations, but the same fetal morbidities.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ GDM does not cause congenital malformations; pre-existing DM does — because of when the hyperglycemia occurs relative to organogenesis. Insulin needs FALL in trimester 1 and after delivery, and RISE steeply in trimester 3. Glyburide crosses the placenta; insulin does not. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated — use beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers. Retinopathy that worsens in pregnancy usually settles after delivery without permanent damage, but screen pre-conception, during, and within the first postpartum year. Fetal death risk is low (0.6–4.8%) — malformation risk is the greater concern.

blocks.html: 1. Pre-existing diabetes before pregnancy

• Pre-conception diabetes (type 1 diabetes or type 2 diabetes (T2DM)) is present from conception, throughout organogenesis (weeks 3–16+), often before pregnancy is even known
  • Fetal death risk is low (0.6–4.8%) — malformation risk is the greater concern
  • Congenital malformations: YES — depends on glycated hemoglobin (A1c) at conception
    • 1.7–9.4% vs. 2–4% background (major malformations)
    • tight control before conception ↓ anomalies by ~70%
  • Pre-conception care
    • Target A1c ≤ 7%, ideally ≤ 6.5%, BEFORE conception
    • prescribe folic acid · screen for diabetic retinopathy

blocks.alt: periconceptional a1c vs risk of congenital anomaly.png
blocks.cap: Absolute risk of a congenital anomaly climbs steadily with periconceptional A1c

blocks.html: 2. Congenital malformations and other infant morbidities
• Congenital malformations (pre-existing DM only) — grouped by system, which is how they are recalled

blocks.alt: critical periods of fetal development - organogenesis timeline.png
blocks.cap: Critical periods of development: most major structural defects arise in weeks 3 to 8, often before pregnancy is known

rows:
neural tube defects — spina bifida, anencephaly
cauda equina regression (skeletal)
transposition of the great vessels · coarctation of the aorta · truncus arteriosus · atrial septal defect · pulmonary stenosis · dextrocardia
duodenal atresia · imperforate anus · anorectal atresia · situs inversus totalis

blocks.html:
• Other infant morbidities — these occur in BOTH groups:
    • cesarean section (32–45%) · prematurity (15% before week 34) · fetal distress (9–28%) · macrosomia > 4 kg (9–28%)
    • small for date (2–8%) if the mother has vascular disease (inadequate placental flow)
    • ↓ calcium · ↑ red blood cell volume · hyperbilirubinemia
    • neonatal hypoglycemia — the baby made ↑ insulin in utero.
3. Insulin requirements across pregnancy

blocks.lead: The bigger the placenta, the higher the hormones and the higher the insulin need.
rows: Placental hormone production rising (prolactin, cortisol, growth hormone)
Irrespective of oral intake; can be ↑↑↑ in T2DM
Warn mothers: glucose can drop, especially while breastfeeding

blocks.alt: insulin requirements across pregnancy - normal vs gestational diabetes.png
blocks.cap: Insulin requirements across pregnancy: a dip near 12 weeks, a steep rise to 36 weeks, and a sharp fall at delivery

blocks.html: 4. Maternal risks with pre-existing diabetes

• Hypertensive disorders · 2× risk of pre-eclampsia (10% vs 5%) · worsening diabetic retinopathy
    • retinopathy that worsens in pregnancy usually settles after delivery without permanent damage · screen pre-conception, during, and within the first postpartum year
  • Worsening diabetic nephropathy — control blood pressure before and during pregnancy
    • ✅ beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers
    • ⛔ angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are CONTRAINDICATED
5. Gestational diabetes (GDM)

• Cause: ↑ insulin resistance from weight gain and placental hormones; the pancreas can only make so much insulin → hyperglycemia
    • transient — usually resolves after delivery · worldwide prevalence ~17%
  • Diagnosis: diagnosed 24–28 weeks — after organogenesis

• Treatment — lifestyle first
    • ↓ carbohydrate, spread over 3 meals + 3 snacks · ~45 g/meal and 20 g/snack (easier for the pancreas to cover than 75 g)
    • post-meal walking, even 10 min
  • Treatment — drugs
    • Insulin is the gold standard and is safe
    • metformin — safe but not very powerful
    • glyburide — likely safe BUT crosses the placenta → neonatal hypoglycemia
    • stop all treatment after delivery
  • Maternal risks: hypertensive disorders in pregnancy · early induction · cesarean section · up to 60% develop T2DM long-term
  • Follow-up: 75 g OGTT at 6 weeks – 6 months postpartum
    • if glucose does not normalise, she had undiagnosed pre-existing T2DM, not GDM
6. Pre-existing diabetes vs. GDM

rows: A1c target · folic acid · retinopathy screen

lectures.name: Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes
lectures.title: Preventing Type 2 Diabetes
lectures.framing: The target population is the grey zone — prediabetes, impaired fasting glucose and impaired glucose tolerance (see 05 - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology). The lecture walks three approaches in order: lifestyle → medication → surgery. No medication is approved in Canada for preventing diabetes — everything below is evidence, not indication.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Lifestyle beats metformin, 58% vs 31% — the single most testable number in this lecture. Thiazolidinediones have the biggest drug effect (62–72%) but the side effect profile that stops you using them. Acarbose's benefit disappears on discontinuation, unlike the durable effect of weight loss. Bariatric surgery is the most effective and still not first line — effectiveness and appropriateness are different questions. And nothing here is actually approved for prevention in Canada.

blocks.html: 1. Lifestyle and diet

• Intensive lifestyle: Low-fat, low-calorie diet + 150 min activity per week
    • risk reduction: 58% — the most effective non-surgical option
    • Even 5% weight loss has benefit
  • Healthy dietary patterns — Mediterranean, Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension, Alternative Healthy Eating Index
    • risk reduction ~20% · a pattern, not a single nutrient

blocks.alt: diabetes prevention program - lifestyle vs metformin vs placebo.png
blocks.cap: Diabetes Prevention Program: lifestyle cut diabetes incidence by 58% and metformin by 31% compared with placebo

blocks.html: 2. Medications

blocks.lead: None is approved for prevention in Canada; these are the drugs with trial evidence.
rows: 31% — roughly half the benefit of lifestyle
More effective in the younger (< 60 years), the obese (BMI > 35), and women with previous gestational diabetes
Limited by adverse effects: peripheral edema, heart failure, osteoporosis and ↑ fractures
Effect did NOT persist after discontinuation
Assessed within obesity effectiveness studies; approved for weight loss, not prevention

blocks.html: 3. Bariatric surgery

• Bariatric surgery: Most effective of all approaches
    • Swedish Obese Subjects study: incident T2DM hazard ratio 0.22 vs usual care over 15 years
  • NOT first line for prevention — cost and procedural risk
  • The two most common in Canada: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (restrictive AND malabsorptive) · sleeve gastrectomy (restrictive only)
    • both 30–35% weight loss · mortality 1 in 500 · covered by the Ontario Health Insurance Plan

blocks.alt: bariatric procedures - gastric band, roux-en-y, sleeve, biliopancreatic diversion - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Bariatric procedures: adjustable gastric band, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy and biliopancreatic diversion

lectures.name: Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL)
lectures.title: Choosing an Antihyperglycemic — Case Analysis
lectures.framing: Every case runs the same four-part analysis: effectiveness → safety → additional benefits → suitability. The drug is chosen by the patient's characteristics, not the glycated hemoglobin (A1c) alone. The session sets out the framework, then four cases that each teach one mechanism, then dosing in kidney disease.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Sulfonylurea secondary failure means the next drug must not be another secretagogue. Linagliptin is the DPP-4 inhibitor that needs no renal adjustment. SGLT2 inhibitors cause genitourinary infections and volume depletion — and cause DKA at normal glucose. AGIs are contraindicated in IBS and inflammatory bowel disease. When insulin requirements exceed anything plausible, stop escalating and look for a receptor-level cause.

blocks.html: 1. The framework

• Efficacy at lowering HbA1c — how much do I need to drop?
    • high: insulin · metformin · GLP-1 analogues · sulfonylureas (SUs) · thiazolidinediones (TZDs)
    • moderate: DPP-4 inhibitors · SGLT2 inhibitors · alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (AGIs)
  • Effect on weight — does the patient need to lose weight, or are they already cachectic?
    • loss: glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) · gain: SU, TZD, insulin
  • Risk of hypoglycemia — do they live alone, drive, eat irregularly, or fear hypoglycemia?
    • Only the secretagogues carry real risk
  • Cardiovascular / renal benefit — established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
    • SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1RAs
  • Special populations — renal or hepatic impairment? See section 6
  • Practical factors — cost · injection vs oral · dosing frequency · adherence — often the deciding factor

blocks.alt: sites of action of antihyperglycemic drug classes - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Where each antihyperglycemic class acts: beta cell secretagogues, sensitizers at muscle, fat and liver, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors in the gut, and incretin agents on gastric emptying and glucagon

blocks.html: 2. Case 1 — hyperglycemia refractory to insulin

• Patient: 46-year-old woman · BMI 45.6 → 16.9 · A1c 14% · insulin > 50 units/kg/day
  • Key factors
    • cachexia with extreme insulin requirement
    • acromegaly-like facies, extensive acanthosis nigricans, skin tags, vitiligo
    • urinary tract infection on empagliflozin · H. pylori triple therapy
  • Mechanism tested: Severe insulin resistance syndrome — when escalating insulin fails, the problem is at the receptor, not the dose
  • What to do
    • ask what explains resistance this extreme
    • note SGLT2 inhibitors → glucosuria → genitourinary infection
    • and that SU + TZD + insulin stack weight gain and hypoglycemia
3. Case 2 — Samuel: adherence and weight

• Patient: 47-year-old man · A1c 8.3% · dyslipidemia · +12 lb · travels constantly · irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
  • Key factors: forgets twice-daily metformin · needs weight loss · eats at consistent times
  • Mechanism tested: matching dosing frequency to lifestyle
  • What to do
    • favour once-weekly GLP-1RAs or once-daily agents with weight loss
    • ⛔ AGIs are contraindicated in IBS · and are taken three times daily
4. Case 3 — Nancy: secondary failure and fear of hypoglycemia

• Patient: 62-year-old woman · A1c 7.1% → 7.9% on max metformin + gliclazide · +5 lb · unemployed · refuses needles · fears hypoglycemia · eats irregularly
  • She wants: glycemic control · weight loss · low hypoglycemia risk · affordable · oral
  • Mechanism tested: Sulfonylurea secondary failure — the K⁺/ATP channel mechanism desensitizes over time
  • What to do
    • do not swap to another secretagogue (glyburide or repaglinide share the mechanism)
    • needs an agent with no hypoglycemia risk, oral, affordable

blocks.alt: sulfonylurea mechanism - beta-cell k-atp channel.png
blocks.cap: Sulfonylureas and meglitinides close the beta-cell K-ATP channel, depolarising the cell and releasing insulin

blocks.html: 5. Case 4 — Albert: SGLT2 inhibitor, kidney injury and shock

• Patient: 72-year-old man in intensive care with acute kidney injury and shock
    • on canagliflozin + hydrochlorothiazide + valsartan — a triple volume-depleting combination
    • 18 months of falls from postural hypotension · foot swelling, ↓ urine output, nausea, shortness of breath
  • Mechanism tested
    • SGLT2i → glucosuria → osmotic diuresis → volume depletion → prerenal acute kidney injury
    • plus euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
  • What to do
    • recognise that the falls were the warning sign
    • hold the SGLT2 inhibitor and diuretic · check ketones regardless of glucose

blocks.title: Euglycemic DKA — the SGLT2 inhibitor trap
blocks.html: DKA can occur with a near-normal blood glucose, because urinary glucose loss blunts the hyperglycemia you would normally use as your trigger to test. Suspect it in any unwell patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor and check ketones regardless of the glucose reading.
6. Antihyperglycemics and kidney function

blocks.lead: (Shah BR et al. Can J Diabetes 2024;48:415-424) — as estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR, mL/min/1.73 m²) falls:
rows: Stepwise dose reduction — full dose (2,550 mg) at ≥ 45 · max 1,000 mg at 30–44 · 500 mg at 15–29 · avoid < 15 or dialysis
Glyburide is avoided once eGFR < 60; gliclazide, glimepiride and repaglinide need no change down to 30 · dose reduction may be needed at 15–29 · avoid < 15
Most need dose reduction (sitagliptin 50 mg at 30–44, 25 mg < 30 · saxagliptin 2.5 mg < 45, avoid < 15) — EXCEPT linagliptin, 5 mg at every eGFR (non-renal clearance)
"Do not initiate, but can continue" below 30 (canagliflozin), 25 (dapagliflozin), 20 (empagliflozin) · canagliflozin 100 mg and empagliflozin 10 mg below 60
No dose change; GLP-1 RAs and tirzepatide have limited data < 15
No maximum dose; dose reduction may be needed below 45
Cardiorenal benefits persist even where glucose-lowering efficacy falls off — which is why an SGLT2 inhibitor may be continued in CKD for reasons other than glycemic control

blocks.alt: metformin renal excretion and lactic acidosis - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Metformin is excreted unchanged by the kidney, so falling renal function lets it accumulate and risks lactic acidosis

weeks.label: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology

lectures.name: Thyroid and Parathyroid Gland Physiology
lectures.title: Thyroid Hormone Synthesis & Calcium Homeostasis
lectures.framing: Two axes, one shape: a gland reacting to a single sensed variable. For the thyroid that is circulating triiodothyronine (T3) / thyroxine (T4), read by the hypothalamus and pituitary, and the exam turns on iodination coming FIRST, then coupling. For the parathyroid it is ionized Ca2+, read directly by the chief cell's calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), and the exam turns on there being no parathyroid hormone (PTH) receptor in the gut. The lecture covers the thyroid first, then calcium.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ There is no PTH receptor in the gut — PTH raises absorbed calcium only indirectly, through calcitriol. Iodination precedes coupling, and iodide entry is active transport (NIS, then pendrin), never passive diffusion. The goitre of iodine deficiency is not the gland "trying harder" — it is loss of negative feedback → sustained TSH-receptor drive → follicular hypertrophy and hyperplasia, and maternal deficiency is the #1 cause of preventable intellectual disability worldwide. somatostatin inhibits TSH ONLY, not PTH. Calcium is the single discriminator between primary and secondary hyperparathyroidism, and hypocalciuria is what separates FHH from primary. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is anti-TPO, blocking iodination of thyroglobulin, treated with levothyroxine; Graves disease is an activating anti-TSH-receptor antibody with exophthalmos. 99% of body calcium sits in bone as calcium phosphate, and of the 1% in blood 50% is free/ionized — that is the only fraction the CaSR reads and the only fraction that acts.

blocks.html: 1. The thyroid axis and hormone synthesis

• Axis: hypothalamus → thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) from the pituitary → thyroid → T3/T4, which feed back negatively
    • somatostatin inhibits TSH ONLY, not PTH
  • Synthesis, in five steps — iodination precedes coupling, and iodide entry is active transport (NIS, then pendrin), never passive diffusion

blocks.alt: thyroid follicular cell - iodide trap nis and pendrin.png
blocks.cap: Thyroid follicular cell: the iodide trap, with the sodium-iodide symporter on the basolateral side and pendrin on the apical side

rows: sodium-iodide (Na+/I-) symporter (NIS) — active, against the gradient, not diffusion
colloid, on ~330 tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin (660 kD, glycosylated, 2 subunits)
crosses bound to thyroglobulin, then freed by proteases inside the cell

blocks.html: 2. Transport in the blood
• ⚠ T3/T4 need carriers because they are amino acid derivatives with an aromatic structure — they are NOT steroid hormones · unbound, their half-life falls

rows: 75% of both T3 and T4
low affinity (66.5 kD monomer) — but carries 20% of T3 because plasma holds so much of it

blocks.html: 3. T3 vs T4, and action inside the cell

• Most T3 acting on a cell is made inside that cell
    • T4 taken up from serum → converted in the cytoplasm → T3 binds thyroid hormone receptor, a nuclear receptor → the complex acts as a transcription factor at thyroid response elements
    • so the deiodinase ratio in the target tissue, not the serum level, sets local activity.

blocks.alt: thyroid hormone action - deiodinases and nuclear receptor.png
blocks.cap: Thyroid hormone action: T4 converted to T3 by type 2 deiodinase in the cytoplasm, T3 acting on a nuclear receptor

rows: weaker — D3 cannot make T2 out of T4; D2 must make T3 first

blocks.html: 4. Hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism

• Iodine deficiency goitre — not the gland "trying harder": loss of negative feedback → sustained TSH-receptor drive → follicular hypertrophy and hyperplasia
    • maternal deficiency is the #1 cause of preventable intellectual disability worldwide
  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis — anti-TPO, blocking iodination of thyroglobulin · treated with levothyroxine
  • Graves disease — an activating anti-TSH-receptor antibody · exophthalmos
  • Mutations in the thyroid players
    • TBG: abnormal TOTAL T3/T4 with normal FREE hormone → the patient is euthyroid
    • TSH receptor: activating → hyperthyroidism or toxic nodule · inactivating → TSH resistance and hypothyroidism
    • thyroid hormone receptor beta: thyroid hormone resistance — high T3/T4 with a non-suppressed TSH
5. Calcium balance and parathyroid hormone
• 99% of body calcium sits in bone as calcium phosphate; of the 1% in blood 50% is free/ionized — the only fraction the CaSR reads and the only fraction that acts

84 amino acid peptide, full activity in the 1-34 fragment"] C --> D["BONE - DIRECT
up osteoclast resorption
down osteoblast formation"] C --> E["KIDNEY distal convoluted tubule - DIRECT
up ACTIVE Ca2+ reabsorption"] C --> F["KIDNEY - 1-alpha-hydroxylase

rows: ↑ ACTIVE Ca2+ reabsorption — the loop of Henle is PASSIVE and not PTH-controlled

blocks.html:
• The PTH receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor signalling down two arms, both converging on ↑ Ca2+
    • Gsα → cAMP → protein kinase A · Gq11α → phospholipase Cβ → diacylglycerol / inositol trisphosphate
    • promiscuous — it also binds parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP), a growth factor normally made in the prostate, which is why a PTHrP-secreting tumour produces humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy
6. Vitamin D
• Its bone effect flips with the calcium level: Ca2+ LOW → resorption by osteoclasts · Ca2+ HIGH → mineralization by osteoblasts
7. Parathyroid disorders compared

rows: 80% single-gland adenoma, clonal and benign; else 4-gland hyperplasia, rarely carcinoma
gland reacting appropriately to chronic kidney disease (↓ 1α-hydroxylation), vitamin D deficiency, or PTH / vitamin D resistance
inactivating CaSR → curve shifts RIGHT, gland needs a higher Ca2+ to switch off
usually iatrogenic, post-total thyroidectomy (the glands sit on the back of the thyroid); rarely autoimmune

blocks.html:
• Primary hyperparathyroidism = chronic hypercalcemia plus chronic resorption
    • ↑ blood pressure · pancreatitis and stomach ulcers · kidney stones · soft bone · depression and psychosis
  • Calcium is the single discriminator between primary and secondary hyperparathyroidism, and hypocalciuria is what separates FHH from primary
8. Receptor mutations in calcium handling

• PTH receptor, activating → Jansen's metaphyseal chondrodysplasia — short-limbed dwarfism
  • PTH receptor, inactivating → Blomstrand's chondroplasia — early death, defective bone maturation
  • CaSR, inactivating → FHH — hypercalcemia in blood but not urine

blocks.alt: familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (right-shift calcium curve).png
blocks.cap: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia: an inactivating calcium-sensing receptor mutation shifts the PTH response curve to the right, so a higher calcium is needed to suppress PTH to its set point

blocks.html: 9. Hypoparathyroidism, hypercalcemia and hypocalcemia

• Hypoparathyroidism is the syndrome of hypocalcemia
    • perioral numbness · carpopedal spasm · convulsions and tetany · impaired memory and personality change
  • Non-parathyroid hypercalcemia
    • humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (PTHrP from lung and kidney carcinomas) · vitamin D toxicity · sarcoidosis (granulomatous vitamin D activation)
    • milk-alkali syndrome — a metabolic alkalosis with back pain and polyuria

lectures.name: Drugs Affecting Calcium Homeostasis
lectures.title: Drugs Affecting Calcium & Bone Mineral Homeostasis
lectures.framing: The lecture starts with vitamin D, then walks the bone drugs: antiresorptives first, then bone-forming. Choosing between the bone drugs turns on three questions: are you stopping bone loss (antiresorptive) or building bone (anabolic)? · what is the creatinine clearance (CrCl), since bisphosphonates and teriparatide are both out below 30 mL/min while denosumab is not · and which way does the drug push serum calcium.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Every antiresorptive causes hypocalcemia and the one anabolic PTH drug causes hypercalcemia. denosumab is the drug of choice when renal function is poor — it does not depend on the kidney for elimination, unlike the bisphosphonates, which are excreted unchanged and accumulate. Denosumab's effects on bone turnover and bone mineral density are reversible; bisphosphonates stay bound in bone, so their benefit and their ONJ risk persist long after stopping — denosumab carries the higher ONJ risk but that risk falls when the drug stops, and the bisphosphonate risk does not. teriparatide is not associated with ONJ and may even treat it. Every antiresorptive drives calcium down, so every patient on one needs adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D. romosozumab is the one drug in both classes at once, and the one whose contraindication list is short but whose cardiovascular signal is the reason to hesitate.

blocks.html: 1. Vitamin D — a hormone, and how it differs from parathyroid hormone (PTH)

• Vitamin D is a hormone acting on vitamin D receptors
    • those receptors sit on many cells with nothing to do with calcium — macrophages included — which is why granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis activates vitamin D and causes hypercalcemia

rows: no receptors here at all — its gut effect is entirely indirect via calcitriol
resorption when Ca2+ is LOW, mineralization when Ca2+ is HIGH

blocks.html: • Phosphate is the discriminator between vitamin D and PTH at the kidney — vitamin D retains it, PTH dumps it
2. Vitamin D supplements

rows: ergocalciferol (vitamin D2) — plant sources, stored in liver, adipose, muscle
the vegan alternative; not bioequivalent to vitamin D3
cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) — sun on 7-dehydrocholesterol, animal sources, fortified food, stored in liver, adipose, muscle
secondary hyperparathyroidism in stage 3–4 chronic kidney disease with a LOW serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D
when you need PTH shut off fast; works independently of renal function

blocks.html: 3. Therapeutic uses and adverse effects of vitamin D

• Therapeutic uses
    • prophylaxis and cure of nutritional rickets · metabolic rickets and osteomalacia
    • hypoparathyroidism — a calcitriol analogue, because it acts fast
    • secondary hyperparathyroidism — shuts PTH off
    • osteoporosis — the most common use, but ⚠ vitamin D alone does not raise bone mineral density enough
  • Hypervitaminosis D is simply the profile of hypercalcemia, split by time course:
    • acute: nausea and vomiting · anorexia · fatigue · weakness
    • chronic: renal impairment · soft-tissue calcification (kidneys, heart, vessels, skin) · hypertension · possibly arrhythmias
4. Drug targets on the calcium loop

blocks.alt: drug targets in calcium and bone homeostasis.png
blocks.cap: Where each drug class acts on the calcium loop: parathyroid, gut, kidney and bone

blocks.html:
• Developed in this lecture: bisphosphonates and denosumab on the osteoclast · teriparatide and romosozumab on bone formation
  • Named but not developed
    • parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor → calcimimetics (cinacalcet) · vitamin D axis → vitamin D and analogues · kidney → thiazide-like diuretics (↑ Ca2+ reabsorption)
    • osteoclast → also selective estrogen receptor modulators, hormone replacement therapy, calcitonin · osteoblast → also fluoride

blocks.alt: Calcium Homeostasis.png
blocks.cap: The calcium loop with every drug placed on it: vitamin D activation from skin to liver to kidney, PTH's actions on kidney, gut and bone, and where thiazides, teriparatide, romosozumab and the antiresorptives act

blocks.html: 5. Antiresorptive drugs — bisphosphonates and denosumab

rows:
1st generation: etidronate (oral), clodronate, tiludronate
2nd generation: pamidronate (IV), alendronate (oral), ibandronate (oral or IV)
3rd generation: risedronate (oral), zoledronate (IV, once yearly)
potency rises with each generation
Bind hydroxyapatite → taken up by the osteoclast resorbing that surface → inhibit the mevalonate pathway → osteoclast apoptosis

oral once daily (alendronate)
intravenous (IV) once yearly (zoledronate)
empty stomach with water (poor oral absorption, many interactions)
sit or stand upright 30 minutes after the pill

Esophageal / gastric irritation · hypocalcemia · bone and joint pain · flu-like symptoms and nephrotoxicity with IV preparations (the flu-like symptoms are temporary) · osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ) — high-dose 3rd generation, IV > oral, risk ↑ after dental extraction · atypical femoral fracture (AFF) (rare, catastrophic)
creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min · esophageal abnormalities · established or predisposed hypocalcemia
Receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL) inhibitors
denosumab — the only one in Canada, and a HUMAN monoclonal antibody (not humanized like romosozumab)
RANKL is released by osteoblasts and osteocytes and activates receptors on osteoclasts → activation, differentiation, survival. Denosumab blocks all three

gastrointestinal (GI) (nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, flatulence) · back / limb / musculoskeletal pain · hypocalcemia · ↑ risk of infection (cough, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection) · ONJ · AFF

blocks.cap: RANKL released by osteoblasts and osteocytes binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and osteoclasts, the step denosumab blocks

blocks.html: • Every antiresorptive causes hypocalcemia — so every patient on one needs adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D
6. Bone-forming drugs — teriparatide and romosozumab

rows: Recombinant 1–34 amino-terminal fragment of human PTH — the fragment carrying full activity. Intermittent spikes build bone; sustained exposure resorbs it

GI (nausea and vomiting, gastritis) · hypotension, dizziness, headache, leg cramps — short-lived, hours after the injection · hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria — the opposite of the antiresorptives · osteosarcoma in rats (historically capped therapy at 2 years; the United States Food and Drug Administration has since removed the boxed warning)
hypercalcemia · creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min · metabolic bone disease
Humanized monoclonal antibody against sclerostin. Sclerostin inhibits formation AND promotes resorption, so blocking it does both at once → antiresorptive and anabolic
arthralgia · hypocalcemia · ONJ, AFF · cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, stroke, death)

blocks.cap: Intermittent PTH gives net bone formation, sustained PTH gives net bone resorption

blocks.html: • teriparatide inherits PTH's kidney profile: raises renal calcium reabsorption but is phosphaturic like native PTH · also ↑ calcitriol production and ↑ osteoblast survival

blocks.html: The module video says sclerostin inhibits both formation and resorption. Dr. Crowley posted an erratum: sclerostin inhibits formation but PROMOTES resorption. The corrected version is what the chart above uses, and it is the reason blocking sclerostin raises formation and lowers resorption.

lectures.name: Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis
lectures.title: Approach to Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis
lectures.framing: The whole evaluation runs on one test in one direction, then one question splits thyrotoxicosis into its causes: is the gland making hormone, or leaking it? — which is what radioactive iodine (RAI) uptake answers. The lecture goes: presentation → thyroid function tests → thyrotoxicosis → hypothyroidism.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ TSH case-finds, free hormone confirms — and the only reason to break that order is suspected central disease, where TSH and FT4 go together and TSH moves WITH the hormone. RAI uptake answers why, not whether. High uptake = the gland is synthesizing; low uptake = hormone is leaking out of it or coming from a bottle, and low-uptake disease is treated supportively while you watch for the hypothyroid phase. Goiter symmetry is a free discriminator: symmetric points to Graves, asymmetric to nodular disease, and thyroiditis can have no goiter at all. Methimazole is first line for Graves and RAI is first line for nodular disease, because only Graves remits. Levothyroxine's 1-week half-life is why TSH is rechecked at 4 to 6 weeks and not sooner. anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin, and ultrasound are the tests to leave alone in straightforward hypothyroidism.

blocks.html: 1. The pathway — TSH first

• Serum thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) to case-find, free hormone only to confirm and grade.
    • TSH works because primary disease, at the gland, is by far the most common kind, and there TSH moves opposite to the hormone
    • ⚠ that logic inverts in central disease, where pituitary TSH is the broken part and moves with the hormone
    • some labs add free thyroxine (FT4) (and free triiodothyronine, FT3) reflexively when TSH comes back abnormal, so the confirmatory step may already be done for you
