blocks.html: 2. Thyroid disease and how it presents

• Two axes: structure — benign vs malignant · functional vs non-functional · function — hyperthyroid vs hypothyroid (this lecture)
  • Differential template — VITAMIN C & D
    • Vascular · Infection, Inflammation · Trauma · Autoimmune, Acquired, Allergic · Metabolic, Mental health · Iatrogenic (thyroid surgery or radiation; drugs) · Neoplasm (central, via pituitary tumour) · Congenital, Cyst · Degenerative
  • History — thyrotoxic or hypothyroid symptoms plus severity · associated features and severity · risk factors · for hypothyroidism ask about past thyroid treatments
  • Physical exam — signs, severity, and complications: pulse and pulse pressure · goiter and its symmetry · tenderness · eye signs · relaxation phase of the reflexes · skin

rows: thyrotoxicosis = too much thyroid hormone from any cause; hyperthyroidism = thyrotoxicosis from thyroid hormone production
bradycardia, diastolic hypertension with a NARROW pulse pressure, ↓ cardiac output
tachycardia, WIDE pulse pressure, ↑ cardiac output, palpitations
heart failure (edema, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea)
slow relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes (Woltman sign)

myxedema coma, very rare: obtundation and hypothermia, with hypotension, bradycardia, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, hypoventilation. Precipitated by a stressor (myocardial infarction, cold, stopping levothyroxine)
hemodynamic instability / thyroid storm (Graves) · high-output heart failure · visual loss from Graves orbitopathy · mental health crisis

blocks.html: 3. Thyroid function tests — and why central disease is the trap

blocks.alt: hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis - primary secondary tertiary.png
blocks.cap: The hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis

blocks.html:
• The central patterns are the trap: TSH moves the same way as the hormone, or not at all.
    • a normal TSH is only reassuring when the pituitary is presumed intact
    • so the one exception to "stop at a normal TSH" is known pituitary deficiency or a known pituitary mass — order TSH and FT4 together from the start
  • What each test is worth: TSH = case-finding / screening · FT4 (+ FT3) = confirmation, and FT3 grades severity
  • Screen serum TSH when:
    • compatible symptoms · dyslipidemia · anemia · hyponatremia · personal or family autoimmune history · Down syndrome or Turner syndrome · previous thyroid disease or therapy · drugs · pregnancy
    • suspected pituitary/hypothalamic disease — add FT4
  • Limit investigations based on the history and physical
  • Choosing Wisely, the six things to question: least invasive test first · only order tests that will change management · discuss with the patient whether a test is necessary · seek clarification about an unnecessary order · do not order tests for the learning experience · do not order tests in anticipation of preceptor preference
4. Thyrotoxicosis — finding the cause

blocks.alt: three sources of thyrotoxicosis - production, release of preformed hormone, exogenous - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The three sources of thyrotoxicosis: increased production by the gland, release of preformed hormone from a damaged gland, or hormone from outside the thyroid

rows: female, age ~30–50, family history of autoimmune disease (especially thyroid), iodine load
iodine deficiency moving to sufficiency, or an iodine load
gradually progressive, MILDLY thyrotoxic, neck mass or masses
tenderness, pain, and odynophagia (subacute); thyrotoxic in all

blocks.html:
• Eye findings split two ways
    • stare (decreased blink), lid retraction, lid lag → any thyrotoxicosis — these are adrenergic, not autoimmune
    • proptosis, periorbital edema, inflammation, diplopia, visual loss → Graves orbitopathy specifically — and visual loss is an OCULAR EMERGENCY
  • Graves orbitopathy mechanism: increased volume of the retro-orbital connective tissue and extraocular muscles, from inflammation, edema, accumulation of extracellular glycosaminoglycans, and increased adipocytes
    • the major risk factor is SMOKING, which also predicts worsening after radioactive iodine · Graves dermopathy is the skin counterpart
  • Investigations for the cause — clinically, with or without:
    • TSH receptor antibody (TRAb) — sensitive AND specific for Graves, a simple blood test, but not covered by the Ontario Health Insurance Plan
    • RAI uptake and scan — best single test for the ETIOLOGY of thyrotoxicosis · relatively expensive · a 2-day test · contraindicated in pregnancy

• Iodine loads (e.g. iodinated contrast) cut both ways — and they suppress RAI uptake, so a scan done after contrast reads falsely low
    • Wolff-Chaikoff effect: the normal gland ↓ hormone production under an iodine load, then escapes to a new euthyroid steady state · underlying subclinical Hashimoto's may not escape → HYPOthyroidism
    • Jod-Basedow phenomenon: autonomous tissue (toxic nodules) or mild subclinical Graves' does not show Wolff-Chaikoff and uses the iodine to make too much hormone → HYPERthyroidism

blocks.cap: Radioactive iodine uptake scans: diffuse high uptake in Graves, a single hot nodule in toxic adenoma, several hot nodules in toxic multinodular goiter, almost no uptake in thyroiditis

blocks.html: 5. Subclinical hyperthyroidism

• TSH ↓, FT4 and FT3 normal · same causes as overt hyperthyroidism
  • linked to bone loss and atrial fibrillation
  • Treatment: treat if older and/or TSH lower · monitor if younger and/or TSH borderline low
  • rarely assay interference — look up interfering substances and repeat
6. Treating thyrotoxicosis
• Supportive care is worth considering in everyone; lowering hormone production is a risks, benefits, and patient-preference conversation

rows: supportive only, plus monitoring for the HYPOTHYROID phase
thyroiditis burns out; for exogenous disease, remove the excess

often 1st line for Graves disease, because Graves is the one that can remit. ~4–6 weeks to euthyroidism. Rare but serious: agranulocytosis, liver dysfunction, drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus. can cause birth defects

often 1st line for toxic adenoma or TMNG; used in Graves if no remission. Permanent cure, but high risk of permanent hypothyroidism. Takes ~6–12 weeks, and ~10% need a 2nd treatment. may worsen Graves eye disease, especially in smokers; ⛔ cannot be used in pregnancy
rarely used. Reserved for a large symptomatic goiter, suspected coincident malignancy, intolerance of antithyroid drugs in pregnancy, or life-threatening thyroid storm refractory to medical treatment

blocks.html: 7. Hypothyroidism

• Cause: Hashimoto's thyroiditis — female, family history of autoimmune disease, iodine load · symptoms highly variable and non-specific · goiter, but signs are not sensitive
    • the rest of the differential: drugs (lithium, amiodarone) · removal or destruction of thyroid tissue (surgery, radioactive iodine) · central — ↓ pituitary/hypothalamic stimulation from trauma, surgery, tumour, infiltrative disease
    • if there is no treatment history and no pituitary risk, you may simply assume Hashimoto's
  • Tests to leave alone
    • anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) / anti-thyroglobulin — sensitive for Hashimoto's, less specific, and almost never influence clinical decisions in hypothyroidism
    • ultrasound — Hashimoto's has characteristic features but ultrasound is not sensitive, not specific, and not required · only for a coincident nodule found on exam
  • Treatment: oral levothyroxine once daily, ~1.5 mcg/kg/day, titrated to a normal TSH
    • half-life = 1 week, which is why you wait 4–6 weeks between dose changes
    • start low and titrate up if elderly or with heart disease
    • ≥ 1 hour before and ≥ 2 hours after eating · 4 hours away from calcium, iron, magnesium, or a multivitamin · any convenient time of day they will actually remember, such as bedtime
  • Follow-up: serum TSH every 4–6 weeks until normal · ⚠ do not monitor FT4/FT3 once you are the one replacing them
  • Subclinical hypothyroidism
    • TSH ↑ (usually < 10–20), FT4 and FT3 normal · may resolve spontaneously, especially TSH < 10 in the elderly
    • no evidence of benefit from treatment, except pregnancy · consider if TSH > 10 or anti-TPO positive (both raise progression risk), or as a therapeutic trial for possible symptoms

lectures.name: Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hyperparathyroidism and Hypoparathyroidism
lectures.title: Hyperparathyroidism, Hypoparathyroidism & the Calcium Panel
lectures.framing: You do not diagnose these from the calcium alone - you read the pattern across four tests at once: parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcium, phosphate, vitamin D. Correct for albumin, then always send a PTH: those two steps decide the entire workup. The lecture runs calcium → hypercalcaemia → hyperparathyroidism → hypocalcaemia → hypoparathyroidism.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Correct for albumin, then always send PTH. Phosphate separates primary from tertiary when calcium cannot - primary drops it because PTH makes the kidney waste phosphate, tertiary raises it because the failing kidney cannot excrete it. PTH direction separates true hypoparathyroidism from the pseudo forms, and pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism is the trap: Albright's phenotype with a completely normal panel. Vitamin D deficiency is the commonest cause of hypocalcaemia, and it is the one where phosphate is LOW rather than high.

blocks.html: 1. Serum calcium and the albumin correction
• Only the free (ionized) calcium is active, and much of the total rides on albumin - so correct the total for albumin first
$$\huge corrected\_calcium = measured\_calcium + 0.02 * (40 - measured\_albumin) $$

blocks.alt: calcium regulation - pth vitamin d kidney bone and gut.png
blocks.cap: Calcium regulation: low calcium raises PTH, which acts on bone and kidney, and calcitriol from the kidney raises gut absorption

blocks.alt: Approach to Hypocalcemia and Hypercalcemia.png
blocks.cap: Calcium, then PTH, then phosphate: the low side splits into hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency and pseudohypoparathyroidism; the high side into malignancy, FHH, primary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism by fractional calcium excretion

blocks.html: 2. Hypercalcaemia

• Causes - over 90% of all hypercalcaemia is hyperparathyroidism or malignancy
    • PTH high or inappropriately normal → PTH-mediated: primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism · familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH)
    • PTH suppressed → PTH-independent:
      • malignancy: metastases - breast · humoral PTH-related protein - lung, kidney, adult T-cell leukaemia · lymphokines - myeloma
      • vitamin D related: exogenous, or granulomatous sarcoid and tuberculosis
      • immobilisation on a background of Paget's, thyrotoxicosis or adrenal insufficiency
      • thiazides · milk-alkali syndrome · acromegaly · phaeochromocytoma · parenteral nutrition
  • Presents as
    • Stones, bones, groans, moans, thrones, muscle tone, psychiatric overtones · often asymptomatic, found on a routine panel
    • short QT, Osborn wave, bradycardia, atrioventricular block · weakness and hyporeflexia · nephrolithiasis · pancreatitis · confusion and apathy

blocks.alt: hypercalcemia ECG findings.png
blocks.cap: Hypercalcaemia on ECG: a short QT interval and an Osborn wave (arrows), both gone once the same patient's calcium is normalized

blocks.html:
• Investigations
    • 1. Corrected calcium, then PTH - always, and it is what decides the whole workup
    • 2. 24-hour urine calcium + creatinine → fractional excretion of calcium (FE_Ca) if PTH is not suppressed
    • 3. dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (bone density scan) · renal ultrasound · vitamin D

blocks.html:
• Treatment - admit if corrected calcium is over 3 mmol/L
    • 1. Volume repletion, assume a 4-6 L deficit, normal saline
    • 2. Forced diuresis: 4-10 L normal saline + furosemide + potassium, only once well hydrated - LOOP diuretics only, NEVER thiazides, which cause hypercalcaemia
    • 3. intravenous zoledronate
    • 4. calcitonin - tachyphylaxis at 24-48 hours, a bridge not a treatment
    • 5. prednisone 40-60 mg/day where steroids reduce vitamin D activation: myeloma, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, vitamin D toxicity
3. Hyperparathyroidism: primary, secondary, tertiary

rows: 80% parathyroid adenoma; also hyperplasia, carcinoma, familial
chronic kidney disease (CKD) - the kidney cannot make vitamin D, so PTH rises to compensate
Secondary gone autonomous - almost always long-standing CKD
As primary, on a CKD background
PTH raised with a normal calcium · estimated glomerular filtration rate and creatinine identify the CKD driving it · phosphate, 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OH-D)
High PTH with HIGH calcium and HIGH phosphate on a CKD background · parathyroid imaging before surgery
Mild: asymptomatic and over 50 → no treatment · drug therapy: bisphosphonates, denosumab, estrogen, cinacalcet · symptomatic → surgery · hydrate, avoid thiazides and lithium
Treat the CKD · phosphate binders, activated vitamin D
Resolves if the kidney is fixed

blocks.html:
• Primary vs FHH - both have a high calcium with a high or normal PTH, so the urine decides: >0.02 primary, <0.01 FHH
    • 0.01-0.02 is an overlap zone: recheck off thiazides, with normal magnesium and 25-OH-D over 50
$$\huge FE_{Ca} = \frac{Urine\ Ca \times (Serum\ Creatinine / 1000)}{Serum\ Ca \times Urine\ Creatinine}$$

• Parathyroidectomy in primary hyperparathyroidism - any ONE of:
    • calcium over 0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit · bone mineral density T-score < −2.5 at lumbar spine, femoral neck, total hip or one-third radius · vertebral fracture · creatinine clearance under 60 mL/min · 24-hour urine calcium over 10 mmol/day with increased stone risk · nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis · age under 50

blocks.alt: hyperparathyroidism hand x-ray - subperiosteal erosions.png
blocks.cap: Hand X-ray in hyperparathyroidism: subperiosteal erosions of the finger bones

blocks.html: 4. Hypocalcaemia

• Causes, sorted by phosphate
    • PTH deficient: calcium ↓, phosphate HIGH, PTH low
    • PTH resistant: calcium ↓, phosphate HIGH, PTH high
    • vitamin D deficient: calcium ↓, phosphate LOW, PTH high - the commonest of the three
    • minor: hypoalbuminaemia · hypomagnesemia · pancreatitis · tumour lysis · rhabdomyolysis · sepsis
  • Presents as
    • QT PROLONGATION → torsades de pointes · tetany · paraesthesia · brain fog
    • acute: severe → tetany (perioral paraesthesias, carpopedal spasm, laryngeal spasm, seizures, palpitations) · mild → Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs
    • chronically: emotional instability, anxiety, brain fog, paraesthesias · cataracts, dry skin, brittle nails · overtreatment → movement disorders, nephrolithiasis
    • why: low calcium lets sodium channels depolarise more easily
  • Treatment (acute) - only for corrected calcium <1.9 mmol/L with neurological (tetany, seizure, carpopedal spasm) or cardiac (prolonged QT) signs
    • 1-2 g of 10% calcium gluconate in 50 mL 5% dextrose in water over 15-20 minutes, then 1-3 mg/kg/h
    • cardiac monitoring · correct the magnesium
5. Hypoparathyroidism and the pseudo forms

rows: Post-parathyroidectomy 75% · non-surgical 25%: autoimmune, infiltrative, post-radiation, metastatic
CATS go numb - convulsions, arrhythmia, tetany, spasm, numbness · Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs
As hypoparathyroidism, plus in type 1A the Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype: round face, short stature, short metacarpals and metatarsals
Low PTH with low calcium · phosphate high · check magnesium
High PTH with low calcium - the receptor, not the gland · phosphate high
calcitriol 0.25 mcg twice daily, keep 25-OH-D >75, aim LOW-normal calcium · 1-2 g elemental calcium in divided doses · thiazide · recombinant human PTH (approved in the US and Europe)
Lifelong; monitor for ectopic calcification · keep the calcium-phosphate product under 4.4 mmol²/L²

blocks.html:
• ⚠ Hypoparathyroidism must persist 6 months after surgery before you call it permanent
  • ⚠ Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism has the same phenotype with a completely normal panel

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Chronic hypocalcaemia: calcitriol + 1–2 g elemental Ca, and a thiazide ↓ urine calcium (↓ stone risk) — the one setting where a thiazide is wanted
  • Monitor for ectopic calcification: renal ultrasound (nephrocalcinosis) · head MRI (basal ganglia calcification)

lectures.name: Pathology of Thyroid Masses
lectures.title: Thyroid Masses: Clinical Evaluation and Pathology
lectures.framing: Most thyroid nodules are benign (0.1% annual incidence, 10% lifetime probability), so the job is not to find cancer in every nodule but to stratify which nodule earns a biopsy and which biopsy earns an operation.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ TSH is the first test, because a low TSH diverts you to an RAI scan and a hot nodule is benign; a normal or high TSH goes to ultrasound and TI-RADS. FNA cannot tell a follicular adenoma from a follicular carcinoma (identical nuclei, and only invasion separates them), but it diagnoses papillary carcinoma outright, because in PTC the nuclei are the diagnosis. Graves makes papillary projections without atypia - architecture alone does not mean papillary carcinoma. Amyloid in a thyroid tumour is calcitonin, and means medullary carcinoma, which is RET point mutation while PTC is RET-PTC translocation. Anaplastic carcinoma is what a well-differentiated cancer becomes, and it is the one that will not take up iodine. Needle core biopsy is the wrong instrument for the neck FOR DIAGNOSING A NODULE - ⚠ but it is the preferred instrument when the diagnosis needs a marker panel off the specimen, which is anaplastic carcinoma and lymphoma. Punch biopsy is for skin. Child, male, first-degree family history, and neck radiation are the clinical risk factors that raise the pre-test probability before any imaging.

blocks.html: 1. The four inputs

• Four inputs stack into one decision: clinical risk, biochemistry, imaging, and fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) - together they give risk-adapted management
    • none of them is read alone
    • the order is fixed: thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) first, then imaging, then the needle
2. Urgent presentations

• Urgent presentations of thyroid CANCER (the nodules case session): short of breath or unable to breathe (airway narrowing or obstruction) · difficulty swallowing · unexplained continued pain · systemic symptoms of metastases (lung, bone)
3. Differential and cancer risk

• ⚠ Do not forget the anatomy: a mass in the thyroid area is not always thyroid - also consider parathyroid, lymph node, skin, and soft tissue
  • Risk factors for cancer in a patient with a nodule
    • child · male · family history in a 1st-degree relative · neck exposure to radiation
  • Symptoms: dysphagia · hoarseness · stridor · growth
  • Signs: firm and/or fixed mass · suspicious lymph nodes
4. Risk stratification: TSH, then ultrasound

• TSH first, because a low TSH sends you to a radioactive iodine (RAI) scan before any ultrasound
    • a HOT nodule is never cancer and stops there, while a COLD nodule comes back to the ultrasound and is scored like any other nodule
    • normal or high TSH → ultrasound + Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) score, which sets the size at which to biopsy

blocks.html: 5. Sampling the nodule

rows: Fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) - 22 gauge or smaller

The neck, and the thyroid especially: safer, and no tumour seeding. Minimally invasive, quick, inexpensive, safe, well tolerated, preserves quality of life. needs expertise. Also the choice in a very ill patient

minimal use in the neck (large bore → tumour seeding and hematoma). Preferred for breast cancer, to see invasion, and may be preferred for lymphoma. Also preferred over FNAB in suspected anaplastic carcinoma, which needs a wide panel of markers, so it needs tissue volume FNAB may not deliver
more morbidity and pain, needs an operating room. not done for the thyroid, because it is vascular - surgery there means lobectomy or thyroidectomy

blocks.html:
• Reading an FNAB report - three parts
    • Adequacy: "satisfactory for evaluation" means it is a good aspirate
    • Diagnosis: e.g. benign follicular nodule, risk of malignancy 0–3% · or positive for malignancy, papillary carcinoma, risk of malignancy 97–99%
    • Observations: what is actually under the microscope - colloid and sheets of follicular cells, or powdery chromatin, nuclear grooves, pseudoinclusions, micronucleoli, crowding
    • then correlate it with the clinical picture and the ultrasound TI-RADS risk - the report is one of four inputs, not the answer
6. Risk-adapted management

rows: Ultrasound surveillance with or without repeat biopsy
insufficient or some indeterminate cytology · benign cytology but high-risk ultrasound (TR5)

blocks.html: • A benign cytology does not end the conversation if the ultrasound is TR5 - the discordance is what triggers the repeat biopsy
7. Thyroid neoplasms

rows: Encapsulated, well-circumscribed, PUSHING border; microfollicles; NO capsular invasion, NO lymphovascular invasion, NO nuclear atypia
Diagnosis is by NUCLEAR features: enlarged, elongated, irregular contours, grooves, clearing, inclusions. Classic type adds papillary architecture on fibrovascular cores. Often multifocal
good: 93% at 10 years. Spreads via lymphatics to locoregional nodes, which may be the initial presentation
Like an adenoma, but with INVASION: growth into adjacent normal thyroid (focal or diffuse) and/or lymphatic or angioinvasion. Lacks nuclear atypia
Sheets of malignant cells, NO follicle formation, angioinvasion, extrathyroidal extension into neck soft tissue
BRAF testing matters - a BRAF inhibitor may be tried

very aggressive, often lethal. Rapidly expanding neck mass; arises by progression OF a well-differentiated carcinoma; infiltration often prevents adequate surgical removal, and it does not respond to RAI so external beam is used
Infiltrative; nests, cords, trabeculae - NOT papillae; amyloid deposition, which IS calcitonin; negative for thyroid markers
RET POINT mutations (not a translocation, unlike papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC))
frequent metastasis, poorer prognosis. Monitor serum calcitonin for recurrence

blocks.html:
• The single most testable limitation of fine needle aspiration (FNA): a follicular adenoma and a follicular carcinoma have identical nuclei, so FNA cannot separate them
    • the distinction is invasion, which needs the resected specimen
    • the opposite is true of papillary carcinoma, whose nuclear features are diagnostic and are readily seen on FNA

blocks.cap: Follicular carcinoma and follicular adenoma side by side: the nuclei look the same, so FNA cannot tell them apart

blocks.alt: papillary thyroid carcinoma nuclei vs normal follicle cells histology.png
blocks.cap: Normal thyroid follicle cell nuclei next to papillary thyroid carcinoma nuclei, whose features are diagnostic on FNA

blocks.html: 8. Pathology of the benign nodules

rows: Nodules of varying size, hyperplastic follicular cells at different functional levels - some more, some less, so the net result is usually EUTHYROID. No atypia. Enlarged, colloid-rich follicles, uniform nuclei. Degenerative changes are common: cystic change, hemorrhage, fibrosis, calcification
autoimmune: antibodies bind TSH receptors on ALL follicle cells, driving both hormone production and follicle-cell PROLIFERATION

Diffusely enlarged, cellular, hyperplastic; NO atypia with or without chronic inflammation. Hyperplastic follicle cells form PAPILLARY PROJECTIONS with no atypia - the trap against papillary carcinoma. Extrathyroidal: ophthalmopathy 25–50%, pretibial myxedema 0.5–4%

Diffuse chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and HURTHLE CELLS - follicle cells that acquire abundant pink cytoplasm and larger nuclei, the same cell looking different (metaplasia). Early on, released stored colloid can cause THYROTOXIC symptoms; the gland may be enlarged or nodular, then becomes fibrotic and small

blocks.html: 9. Treatment of thyroid cancer

rows: well-differentiated carcinoma with high recurrence risk - useless in poorly differentiated disease, which does not take up iodine

blocks.html:
• Radioactive iodine by American Thyroid Association (ATA) recurrence risk (case session): low → not recommended (under 1 cm), "not routine" (1–4 cm), "consider" (over 4 cm) · intermediate → "generally favoured" · high → recommended (gross extrathyroidal extension, incomplete resection, distant metastases)
  • Follow-up after treatment: ultrasound within 6–12 months of initial therapy, then periodically - remaining lobe and cervical lymph nodes · biopsy a suspicious node over 8–10 mm in its smallest dimension
10. Reporting, staging and prognosis

• The surgical pathology report is what closes the case
    • its elements: tumour type · unifocal or multifocal · size · encapsulated or not · capsular invasion, focal or extensive · lymphatic invasion · angioinvasion · extrathyroidal extension · lymph node metastasis, with the size of the largest and whether there is extranodal extension · margin status
    • together they decide the need for additional surgery, RAI, external beam radiation, and chemotherapy, plus local recurrence risk and prognosis
  • Staging turns on age 55 in differentiated thyroid cancer
    • 10-year disease-specific survival: stage I 98–100%, stage II 85–90%, and over 55, stage III 60–70%, stage IV under 50%

lectures.name: Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Osteoporosis
lectures.title: Osteoporosis: Diagnosis, Risk and Treatment
lectures.framing: You can diagnose osteoporosis three ways, and only one of them involves a bone density scan. Once diagnosed, treatment choice turns on which fracture site you need to prevent and whether the patient has already failed or been harmed by an antiresorptive (a drug that slows bone breakdown).
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis on its own - but skull, hands, feet and ankles do not count, and neither does a genuinely traumatic fracture. T-score compares to a young adult, Z-score to age-matched peers; only the T-score diagnoses. raloxifene and teriparatide have no hip fracture data - reach for a bisphosphonate, denosumab, or estrogen when the hip is the concern. Every anabolic course must be followed by an antiresorptive, at 1 year for romosozumab and 2 for teriparatide. Osteonecrosis of the jaw has a definition with a clock in it: exposed bone unhealed at 8 weeks, and dental work goes first. Groin or thigh pain in a patient on a bisphosphonate is an impending atypical femoral fracture, not arthritis.

blocks.html: 1. Why it matters: the treatment gap

• A fragility fracture is the diagnosis - yet only 15% of patients are treated after a fragility fracture, against 80% who get a beta blocker after a heart attack.
  • Burden: osteoporotic fractures cause 153,400 events a year in Canadian women - more than heart attack (49,220), stroke (22,700) and breast cancer combined
    • lifetime risk of hip fracture over age 50 is 12.1%
  • One year after a hip fracture
    • 80% cannot carry out more than one instrumental activity of daily living · 40% cannot walk independently · 29% are dead
    • five-year mortality: 23.5% after hip fracture · 15.7% after vertebral fracture
2. Diagnosis

cols: Diagnose osteoporosis if any ONE holds
rows: irrespective of any other measure, whatever the bone mineral density (BMD) says. EXCLUDING fractures of the skull, hands, feet and ankles, and any fracture with real trauma
in the absence of a fragility fracture and with a T-score above −2.5

blocks.html: 3. Symptoms: a silent disease

• Osteoporosis is a silent disease. The large majority are asymptomatic, and symptoms come from fractures
  • ⚠ The exception is the spine: up to two thirds of vertebral fractures are asymptomatic, found incidentally on x-ray
    • graded on vertebral height loss, with > 25% loss considered significant
    • over time they produce kyphosis

blocks.alt: vertebral fracture grading - wedge biconcave crush.png
blocks.cap: Vertebral fracture grading by height loss: wedge, biconcave and crush shapes, grade 1 to grade 3

blocks.html: 4. Investigations and fracture risk

rows: a misnomer: bone mineral content divided by AREA, not volume. It is a surrogate measure for fracture
the patient's BMD against a young healthy adult - the score that diagnoses
the patient's BMD against an age-matched population

blocks.alt: osteopenia vs. osteoporosis.png
blocks.cap: T-score bands: -1 or more is normal bone, -1 to -2.5 is osteopenia, -2.5 or less is osteoporosis; notice the trabecular holes widening across the three

blocks.html:
• Who gets a bone density scan (Osteoporosis Canada algorithm, postmenopausal women and men ≥ 50): age 50–64 with a previous fracture or ≥ 2 risk factors · 65–69 with 1 risk factor · ≥ 70 with no risk factors · under 70 with no risk factors → no scan, lifestyle only · previous hip or spine fracture, or ≥ 2 fracture events → straight to recommend pharmacotherapy
    • risk factors: previous fracture after age 40 · glucocorticoids (> 3 months in the last year, prednisone > 5 mg daily) · ≥ 2 falls in the last year · parent with a fractured hip · body mass index < 20 kg/m² · secondary osteoporosis · current smoking · alcohol ≥ 3 drinks/day
  • Risk comes from the femoral neck T-score combined with age (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX) Canada 2020 preferred, or the Canadian Association of Radiologists and Osteoporosis Canada tool)
    • 10-year absolute fracture risk: < 10% low · 10–20% moderate · > 20% high
  • Modifiers
    • lumbar spine or total hip T-score ≤ −2.5 → consider the patient at least moderate risk
    • prolonged corticosteroid therapy → up one risk category
    • prior fragility fracture after age 40 → up one risk category
    • prior hip or vertebral fracture, or more than one non-vertebral fragility fracture → high risk
  • Blood tests in the workup:
    • serum calcium corrected for serum albumin · complete blood count · creatinine (many of these drugs are renally cleared) · alkaline phosphatase (bone turnover) · serum thyroid stimulating hormone (hypothyroidism causes bone loss) · 25-hydroxyvitamin D
  • Physical signs that prompt vertebral fracture imaging:
    • prospective height loss > 2 cm · historical height loss > 6 cm · rib-to-pelvis distance ≤ 2 finger-breadths in the midaxillary line · occiput-to-wall distance > 5 cm
5. Decision to treat and lifestyle

• Pharmacotherapy by 10-year fracture risk
    • < 15% or T-score > −2.5 → do NOT recommend pharmacotherapy
    • 15–19.9%, or T-score ≤ −2.5 and age < 70 → SUGGEST pharmacotherapy (intermediate benefit)
    • ≥ 20%, or T-score ≤ −2.5 and age ≥ 70 → RECOMMEND pharmacotherapy (largest benefit)
  • Strong recommendation to treat: hip, vertebral, or more than 2 osteoporosis-related fractures, with greater consideration when the fracture was within the last 2 years
  • Lifestyle treatment:
    • calcium and vitamin D (⚠ not enough on their own to raise BMD) · weight-bearing exercise
    • fall prevention: grab bar in the shower · get rid of loose rugs and uneven steps · avoid lifting heavy objects · no standing on chairs

rows: 600 international units daily, adults 51–70 · 800 international units daily, adults > 70
1200 mg/day for women < 50 and men > 70, as the slide reads (standard teaching is women over 50; check with the lecturer) (about 4 servings of dairy) · 1000 mg/day for men 50–70

blocks.html: 6. Drug therapy: which drug prevents which fracture
*versus placebo · #versus alendronate

• raloxifene covers the spine only, which is what makes it the wrong answer whenever hip protection is the goal
  • teriparatide has no hip data either, despite being anabolic
7. Rare side effects of bisphosphonates and denosumab

rows: rare with bisphosphonates and denosumab. A lesion in the oral cavity with exposed bone where mucosa should be, not healed after appropriate care by 8 weeks, with no prior head, face, or mouth radiation. Risk factors: cancer, obesity, diabetes, oral infection, dental extractions, comorbidities. Between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 100,000 patient-treatment years. Complete dental work BEFORE starting therapy
rare with bisphosphonates and denosumab. Warning sign: dull or aching pain in the groin or thigh, present in 70% of patients

blocks.alt: atypical femoral fracture - features and x-ray.png
blocks.cap: Atypical femoral fracture: major and minor features, with an X-ray of a transverse femoral shaft fracture

blocks.html: 8. Bone-forming (anabolic) therapy

• Indications
    • recent severe vertebral compression fracture · more than 2 vertebral fractures with a T-score < −2.5 · failure of antiresorptive therapy
  • Sequencing - anabolic therapy MUST be followed by an antiresorptive
    • after 1 year for romosozumab · after 2 years for teriparatide
    • the bone you build is lost again if nothing holds it

lectures.name: Overview of Metabolic Bone Disease
lectures.title: Metabolic Bone Disease: Osteomalacia, Paget's & Osteogenesis Imperfecta
lectures.framing: Three diseases of bone that are not osteoporosis, and the lab panel separates all three before any imaging. Osteomalacia is a mineralization defect, Paget's is disordered remodelling, and osteogenesis imperfecta is a collagen gene defect - the lecture takes them in that order.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ ALP is the thread through all three: very high in Paget's, high in osteomalacia, normal in osteogenesis imperfecta. Calcium and phosphate are BOTH low in osteomalacia and BOTH normal in Paget's - that pair alone separates them. Urine calcium is LOW in osteomalacia, which is the opposite of what a stone-former's panel looks like. Proximal myopathy is the osteomalacia feature that osteoporosis never has, and it is what causes the falls. Bone-forming drugs are contraindicated in Paget's - you do not encourage a formation process that is already disordered, which makes zoledronate the answer and teriparatide the trap. Increased hat size and warmth over a bone are Paget's, and blue sclerae with fractures from birth are osteogenesis imperfecta. A young adult with celiac disease, falls, weakness and pseudofractures has osteomalacia, not osteoporosis.

blocks.html: 1. Osteomalacia (adult) / rickets (child)

• Osteomalacia = defect in bone matrix MINERALIZATION, from vitamin D deficiency
    • ⚠ Osteomalacia is routinely mistaken for osteoporosis - the tell is that osteomalacia has overt symptoms while osteoporosis is indolent
    • why vitamin D sits at the centre of it: vitamin D is essential for calcium absorption, and adequate calcium absorption is what prevents secondary hyperparathyroidism and limits bone resorption - take it away and you get both a mineralization defect and a secondary drive to resorb bone
  • Causes - malabsorption is a common one, especially celiac disease

rows: insufficient sunlight · nutritional deficiency · malabsorption (e.g. celiac disease, bariatric surgery) · hydroxylation defects · nephrotic syndrome (lost with protein in the urine)
the liver makes calcifediol (25-hydroxyvitamin D, 25-OH-D) - so chronic liver failure
the kidney makes calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) - so chronic renal failure, stages 3, 4, and dialysis
these drugs ↑ vitamin D catabolism: phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, isoniazid, theophylline, rifampin

blocks.html:
• ⚠ The elderly are set up for it four ways at once
    • vitamin D formation and processing may be impaired · sunlight exposure is limited · dietary sources provide little · adherence to supplements is inconsistent
    • amounts in ordinary products are small and variable: multivitamin 200–1000 IU · calcium tablet with D 120–1000 IU · fortified milk 111–150 IU per cup and fluctuating · supplements 400 and 1000 IU per tablet
    • the main source is still sunlight
  • Presents as
    • weak bones that fracture · bone and joint pain · PROXIMAL muscle weakness (myopathy), which can be severe and cause falls
    • children: bowed legs, lordosis, large forehead
    • positive Chvostek's sign / Trousseau's sign
  • Investigations
    • imaging: pseudofractures (healed microfractures)
    • biopsy: usually not necessary, but is the gold standard

blocks.alt: pseudofractures.png
blocks.cap: Osteomalacia: a pseudofracture (Looser zone) of the medial femoral neck, the same X-ray shown plain and with the lucent band highlighted

blocks.html:
• Treatment - treat the underlying cause: vitamin D supplementation, plus phosphate and calcium if low; it corrects with replacement
    • dosed off the initial 25-OH-D:
      • < 30 nmol/L → 50,000 international units (IU) of ergocalciferol weekly for 12 weeks, then 800–2,000 IU
      • 30–75 nmol/L → 800–2,000 IU daily
      • repeat the level in 3 months, aiming for 75–150 nmol/L
2. Paget's disease of bone

• Paget's disease = localized disorder of bone REMODELLING: ↑ osteoclastic resorption, then osteoblasts respond by making new bone that is structurally abnormal and fragile
    • 5% of the population, and 10% of those over 80
  • Presents as
    • usually ASYMPTOMATIC, found on a routine x-ray or an elevated ALP
    • severe bone pain: pelvis, femur, tibia
    • deformity: bowed tibia · kyphosis · frequent fractures
    • skull: headaches, increased HAT SIZE, deafness
    • increased WARMTH over the bone, from increased vascularity
  • Investigations
    • bone scan for extent · the initial lesion may be destructive and radiolucent · involved bones expanded and denser than normal · multiple fissure fractures
    • signs: cotton wool appearance · Tam o' Shanter sign · blade of grass sign · banana fracture · picture-frame vertebra

blocks.alt: paget disease of bone skull x-ray - cotton wool appearance.png
blocks.cap: Paget disease of bone: enlarged skull with a cotton wool appearance

blocks.alt: paget disease of bone tibia x-ray vs normal - sclerotic and lytic areas.png
blocks.cap: Paget disease of bone in the tibia beside a normal tibia: expanded bone with sclerotic and lytic areas

blocks.html:
• Complications
    • fractures · hypercalcemia with immobility · cranial nerve compression → deafness · spinal cord compression
    • osteosarcoma in 1–3%, signalled by marked bone pain, a new lytic lesion, and a rising ALP
    • high-output congestive heart failure from increased vascularity · osteoarthritis
  • When to treat Paget's, even in an asymptomatic patient, given active disease (↑ ALP or scintigraphy showing active lesions)
    • disease in the skull, long bones, spine, or bone abutting a joint
    • a surgical procedure planned in a pagetic site - the lesions are vascular and can hemorrhage
    • coexisting congestive heart failure, which Paget's vascularity can worsen
  • Treatment
    • analgesia · bisphosphonates, and intravenous (IV) zoledronate beats oral
    • calcitonin loses effect after a few treatments, so is only useful early
    • bone-forming agents are CONTRAINDICATED - the disease is already abnormal formation
    • denosumab has not been studied
3. Osteogenesis imperfecta

• osteogenesis imperfecta = a lack of, or poorly formed, TYPE I COLLAGEN
    • mutations in type I collagen: COL1A1 and COL1A2, 85–90% of cases · 16 subtypes and growing
    • among the more common of the rare bone disorders: 1 in 15,000–20,000 live births
  • Presents as
    • fragility fractures from minimal trauma, starting in utero or at birth
    • short stature · bowing of long bones · basilar skull deformities · scoliosis · pectus excavatum or carinatum · Wormian bones
    • blue sclerae · hearing loss · dentinogenesis imperfecta · joint hypermobility
    • across all types (the deck's table, Patel 2015): blue sclerae 78% · hypermobility 57% · dentinogenesis imperfecta 35% · hearing loss 13% · scoliosis under 30° 16%, over 30° 11% · about 1 fracture a year on average
    • aortic root dilatation and valvular insufficiency
  • Investigations: panel normal, diagnosis is clinical · skeletal x-rays
  • Treatment - IV bisphosphonates (zoledronate) are the mainstay. Optimal duration has not been studied
    • treat the bone disease when there are long bone deformities, vertebral compression fractures, or more than 3 fractures per year
  • Lifelong monitoring:
    • growth and head circumference · yearly spirometry (restrictive lung disease from the skeletal deformity)
    • hearing test, bone mineral density, ECG and echocardiogram every 2 years · skeletal radiographs every 1–2 years
    • neurologic and cranial assessment as symptoms indicate
  • Prognosis: highly variable - type 1 has a normal lifespan, type 2 is lethal in the perinatal period
4. Telling the three apart: the lab panel

rows: VERY high - and it is how the disease is monitored on treatment

lectures.name: Embryology & Histology
lectures.title: Female Genital Histology & Early Embryogenesis
lectures.framing: Two halves that share one idea: structure tells you what can go wrong there. In the histology half, the epithelium at each site predicts its disease - keratinized skin gets skin cancers, and the one place two epithelia meet is the one place cervical cancer starts. In the embryology half, the same teratogen does something completely different depending on the week it arrives, so timing, not the agent, is what the question is really testing.
lectures.keypoints: Keratin and adnexa separate labia majora from minora, and that is the whole histological question. ⭐ The transformation zone is where two epithelia meet, which is why it is where cervical cancer arises and why the cancer can be of either type. Tubular glands mean proliferative and oestrogen; tortuous secretory glands mean luteal and progesterone. The functionalis sheds and the basalis rebuilds it. Fertilization happens in the ampulla, and the ampulla is also where an ectopic most often implants - same widest segment, same reason. The zona pellucida must degenerate before implantation can happen. Syncytiotrophoblast makes hCG; hCG maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over at week 8. Every germ layer descends from the epiblast, and the hypoblast only ever makes the yolk sac lining. Weeks 3 to 8 is the critical period - before it, all or nothing; after it, minor anomalies only.

blocks.html: 1. Vulva

rows: KERATINIZED stratified squamous with hair follicles and eccrine, apocrine, sebaceous glands - i.e. skin
susceptible to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma and lichen sclerosus (the equivalent of balanitis xerotica obliterans on the penis)
NON-keratinized stratified squamous, and usually NO adnexal structures (no hair, no glands)
the keratin and the adnexa are the whole discriminator from labia majora
branching mucus-secreting glands, lined by transitional epithelium and/or squamous metaplasia

blocks.html: 2. Vagina
• vagina, inside out: non-keratinizing squamous (mucosa, barrier) → thick smooth muscle muscularis → adventitia of loose connective tissue with elastic fibres
3. Cervix

• ectocervix: non-keratinizing squamous (faces the vagina)
  • endocervix: mucus-secreting GLANDULAR (lines the canal)
  • Transformation zone: squamous metaplasia where squamous meets glandular
    • the most common site of cervical cancer, and it can be either squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma because both epithelia are present
  • ⚠ Pap test versus cervical biopsy: a pap gives cells with NO information about architecture · a biopsy gives tissue, so architecture can be assessed

blocks.alt: cervix - endocervix transformation zone and ectocervix epithelium.png
blocks.cap: Cervix: glandular endocervix, the transformation zone of squamous metaplasia, and squamous ectocervix, with matching histology

blocks.html: 4. Uterus and the endometrial cycle

• uterus, inside out: endometrium (glands + stroma) → myometrium (thick smooth muscle, contracts in labour) → serosa (peritoneal)
    • functionalis is shed; basalis is NOT, and regenerates the functionalis

rows: TUBULAR glands, endometrium thickening, mitotic figures in glands and stroma
TORTUOUS glands with luminal secretions and secretory vacuoles, primed for implantation

blocks.html:
• endometrial biopsy is indicated for
    • infertility · abnormal uterine bleeding · post-menopausal bleeding, to rule out malignancy · endometrial cells on a pap smear in a woman over 45
5. Fallopian tube
• Fallopian tube, inside out: ciliated and secretory mucosa → smooth muscle muscularis (peristalsis moves ovum and sperm) → serosa
6. Ovary and follicular development

• ovary, outside in: low cuboidal surface epithelium → cortex (stromal cells, germ cells, and the specialized granulosa and theca cells) → medulla (stroma, vessels, nerves) → hilum (where vessels and nerves enter)
    • granulosa cells make the steroid hormones
  • Follicular development, in order: oocyte → primordial follicle → primary follicle → secondary follicle → mature (Graafian) follicle
    • after ovulation the corpus luteum remains and makes progesterone
    • with no fertilization it degenerates into a corpus albicans, a scar

blocks.alt: structure of an ovary - follicle stages and corpus luteum.png
blocks.cap: Structure of an ovary: primordial, primary, secondary and mature follicles, ovulation, corpus luteum and corpus albicans

blocks.html: 7. Week 1: fertilization to implantation
• The first four weeks at a glance:

acrosomal enzymes cross corona radiata and zona pellucida
ZONAL REACTION blocks polyspermy"] --> B["Zygote, 44 + XX or XY"] B --> C["Cleavage - division with NO growth
blastomeres get smaller
MORULA, same size as the zygote"] C --> D["Blastulation, day 4

THE ZONA MUST DEGENERATE FIRST"] E --> F["WEEK 2 - the twos

blocks.html:
• The zona pellucida must degenerate before implantation can happen.
  • Ectopic implantation sites: Fallopian tube 96–98% · ovary 4% · abdominal cavity 1% · internal cervical os 1% · endocervical canal 1%
8. Week 2: the bilaminar disc

rows: forms the amniotic cavity - future ECTODERM, and all three germ layers come from the epiblast

blocks.alt: embryogenesis (bilaminar disc).png
blocks.cap: Week 2 bilaminar disc: epiblast over the amniotic cavity and hypoblast over the yolk sac, wrapped by cytotrophoblast and the hCG-secreting syncytiotrophoblast

blocks.html:
• hCG keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone until week 8, when the placenta takes over.
    • beta hCG is what a pregnancy test detects
    • ⚠ a LOW hCG suggests ectopic pregnancy or a spontaneous abortion
9. Week 3: gastrulation

• Gastrulation in three steps
    • ① epiblast cells invade the hypoblast and replace it → ENDODERM
    • ② epiblast cells migrate laterally and cranially between endoderm and epiblast → intraembryonic MESODERM
    • ③ the epiblast cells left behind → ECTODERM
  • Mesoderm then differentiates into paraxial, intermediate, and lateral plate
    • lateral plate splits into dorsal somatic and splanchnic, with the intraembryonic coelom between them
  • The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural tube
10. Week 4: neural tube closure and folding

• Embryonic folding divides the intraembryonic cavity into pericardial (heart), pleural (lungs), and peritoneal (abdominal organs) cavities
    • reduces the yolk sac to the vitelline duct
  • The heart is the FIRST organ to function, audible by week 4; the lungs are the LAST, only at birth
11. Teratogens: timing is everything

rows: "ALL OR NOTHING" - it either kills the embryo or does nothing at all
THE CRITICAL PERIOD. Cell division, differentiation, organogenesis and morphogenesis all peak → MAJOR congenital anomalies
morphological and functional development peaks → MINOR morphologic anomalies (e.g. a malformed external ear) and functional defects

lectures.name: Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis
lectures.title: The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis
lectures.framing: The axis is three tissues - hypothalamus, anterior pituitary, gonads - and one non-negotiable requirement: gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) must arrive in PULSES. A continuous GnRH signal does not amplify the axis, it shuts it down, which is exactly how a GnRH agonist becomes a chemical castration.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Pulsatility is the whole axis. Continuous GnRH suppresses, which is why an agonist ends up doing the same job as an antagonist but with a dangerous surge first. kisspeptin is the strongest positive input to the pulse generator, and steroids never touch the GnRH neuron directly - they work through interneurons. LH → theca and Leydig; FSH → granulosa and Sertoli, and inhibin brakes FSH alone. The shared α subunit is why the β subunit is what gets measured. Cholesterol to pregnenolone, in the mitochondrion, is the rate-limiting step. Estradiol and progesterone act without further metabolism; testosterone usually does not. Estradiol induces the progesterone receptor, so the order of the cycle is built into the receptors themselves.

blocks.html: 1. The three levels and the two kinds of hypothalamic neuron

blocks.alt: hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis - primary secondary.jpg
blocks.cap: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis

blocks.html:
• hypothalamus makes GnRH
    • made by endocrine and non-endocrine cells, with endocrine, paracrine, autocrine and juxtacrine effects
    • GnRH-I is the mammalian form · GnRH-II, first found in chicken hypothalamus, is also present in humans and differs by three amino acid shifts at positions 5, 7 and 8
  • anterior pituitary makes luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) - both named for their action in the ovary
  • gonads make estrogen, progesterone, testosterone, plus activin and inhibin - inhibin and activin are the FSH-specific feedback arm

rows: across the median eminence into the POSTERIOR pituitary via the pituitary stalk
the portal circulation to the ANTERIOR pituitary

blocks.html: 2. The hypophysial portal system and the median eminence

• The portal route, in order
    • peptides released into the median eminence → primary plexus capillaries (fed by the carotid artery) → hypophysial portal veins in the pituitary stalk (long parallel veins connecting two capillary beds) → secondary plexus supplying the anterior pituitary → hormones act on receptors there (e.g. the GnRH receptor) → LH and FSH enter the same capillaries into the general circulation
  • The median eminence is one of only seven brain regions without a blood-brain barrier - so hypothalamic peptides can leave the brain
    • it is where both halves of the hypothalamus are joined
  • The hypothalamus also regulates food energy expenditure, body weight, fluid intake and balance, blood pressure, thirst, temperature and the sleep cycle, organised into nuclei from the preoptic area to the mammillary nucleus

blocks.alt: hypophyseal portal system - median eminence to anterior pituitary.png
blocks.cap: Hypophyseal portal system: hypothalamic neurons release peptides at the median eminence, portal veins carry them to the anterior pituitary, while other neurons run straight to the posterior pituitary

blocks.html: 3. The GnRH pulse generator

• GnRH neurons spontaneously depolarize in a coordinated fashion, releasing GnRH pulsatilely, which drives pulsatile LH and FSH
    • the capacity is INTRINSIC: cultured GnRH neurons show the same coordinated release in vitro, so the rhythm is not imposed from outside
  • Positive regulators: glutamate, neuropeptide Y, norepinephrine - and kisspeptin is the STRONGEST positive regulator
  • Negative regulators: gamma-aminobutyric acid and endogenous opioid peptides
  • Steroids act INDIRECTLY: estradiol and progesterone do NOT act on the GnRH neuron itself - they change the activity of other neurons that synapse onto it
4. GnRH agonists versus antagonists

rows: initial STIMULATION of the axis → a surge in steroids, then receptor desensitization shuts production down
competitive and reversible block of the pituitary GnRH receptor → no LH or FSH release
men: ↓ LH → rapid ↓ testosterone from the testes · women: ↓ LH → ↓ estradiol from the ovaries

prostate cancer: fast testosterone suppression with no surge, so no antiandrogen is needed - a testosterone surge can flare tumour growth. In vitro fertilization: cetrorelix and ganirelix prevent a premature LH surge and endogenous ovulation during FSH stimulation

blocks.html: • The agonist-versus-antagonist contrast is the highest-yield pharmacology in this lecture, and the reason is entirely kinetic: the agonist has to pass through stimulation to reach suppression, and in prostate cancer that transit is dangerous

blocks.alt: HPG axis.png
blocks.cap: Drug targets on the gonadal axis: GnRH agonists such as leuprolide first stimulate LH and FSH, then suppress them after receptor downregulation, while the antagonist degarelix blocks the pituitary at once

blocks.html: 5. Anterior pituitary: LH and FSH

rows: cholesterol side-chain cleavage - the first step of steroid synthesis
androgen binding protein in the testis, and inhibin from both gonads

blocks.html:
• Both are glycoproteins of two subunits that share the same α subunit
    • so the β subunit determines biologic activity and is what an assay must measure (the α is shared with human chorionic gonadotropin too)
  • Both bind G protein-coupled receptors, which activate adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP
  • inhibin feeds back specifically to the FSH-producing cells, reducing their responsiveness to GnRH - a selective brake on FSH rather than on the whole axis
6. Gonads: steroid synthesis and transport

• Steroids are terpenoid lipids: four fused rings in a 6-6-6-5 arrangement, differing only by the functional groups attached and the oxidation state of the rings
  • The rate-limiting step is the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone, inside the mitochondria

rows: YES - conversion to dihydrotestosterone or estradiol is often required

blocks.html:
• Neither progesterone nor estradiol is stored in the follicle or corpus luteum: both are secreted rapidly into the blood and bound to plasma proteins
  • Estradiol is required to induce progesterone receptors - progesterone cannot act on a tissue oestrogen has not primed first, which is the molecular reason the luteal phase must follow the follicular one
7. Steroid hormone mechanisms of action

rows: steroid crosses the membrane → binds a CYTOPLASMIC receptor → complex moves into the nucleus → the receptor dimer binds the hormone response element (HRE) on DNA → transcription. Slow because new mRNA and protein must be made
the hormone-receptor complex binds other transcription factors (protein-protein interactions) rather than DNA directly → transcription
binds a plasma membrane receptor → intracellular signalling, with no change in gene expression

blocks.html: 8. Regulation of the axis
• Inhibitors of hypothalamic kisspeptin (kiss1 mRNA, in rodents): aging · negative energy status · acute, chronic, cold and light stress · high-fat diet · administration of pro-inflammatory cytokines

lectures.name: Approach to the Menstrual Cycle
lectures.title: The Menstrual Cycle
lectures.framing: One hormone does something no other hormone in the body does: estradiol switches its own feedback from negative to positive. That single switch divides the cycle in two: the follicular phase is built by follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and dismantled by the estradiol it produces; the luteal phase runs on progesterone and lasts a fixed two weeks unless an embryo arrives.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Estradiol is the only hormone here that reverses the sign of its own feedback, and it needs both a level (300–500 pg/mL) and a duration (~48 hours) to do it. Getting one of those two right and the other wrong is the classic distractor. FSH falls during the follicular phase - counter-intuitively, because the follicle it grew is now making the oestrogen that suppresses it. The luteal phase is the fixed half of the cycle; when a cycle is short or long, it is the follicular phase that varies. The corpus luteum regresses after two weeks unless an embryo rescues it, and that regression is menstruation. Aromatization happens in the granulosa cell, on an androgen the theca cell made - remember which receptor sits on which cell and the rest follows.

blocks.html: 1. What each piece contributes

• GnRH and gonadotrophin release are REQUIRED - the deck's point from the first experiment
    • a 24-year-old with Kallmann syndrome - who makes no gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) - had a spontaneous ovulatory menstrual cycle initiated by an invariant intermittent subcutaneous GnRH infusion, 25 ng/kg every 2 hours for 27 days
    • invariant is the point: the pituitary and ovary generate the cycle's shape, given only a steady pulse train
  • So is an ovary - and of course an endometrium - the deck's point from the second
    • ovarian tissue transplanted subcutaneously to the abdomen of a castrated male rhesus monkey showed repetitive ovulatory cycles averaging 28 days
  • GnRH and gonadotrophin pulse frequency and amplitude vary during the cycle
2. Follicular waves

• Women usually have either 2 or 3 waves of follicular development per cycle, not the single tidy recruitment the classic diagram implies
  • There is intrinsic regulatory control of follicular development exerted by the ovary itself
3. The two phases side by side

blocks.html: 4. Follicular phase: the two-cell mechanism and the switch

rows: estradiol, by AROMATIZATION of that testosterone

blocks.html:
• Neither cell can make estradiol alone
    • the theca has the LH receptor and makes the substrate · the granulosa has the FSH receptor and the aromatase
    • so FSH-driven follicular growth and LH-driven oestrogen production are the same process described from two sides

blocks.html:
• The switch: below threshold estradiol suppresses FSH · held above 300–500 pg/mL for about 48 hours it flips to feed-forward and triggers the luteinizing hormone (LH) surge.
    • the surge triggers ovulation

blocks.html: 5. Luteal phase and the endometrium

rows: proliferation and thickening - and it induces the progesterone receptors that make the next phase possible
thickens and primes the endometrium, secreting glycogen and glycoproteins

lectures.name: Testicular and Ovarian Function
lectures.title: Testicular and Ovarian Function
lectures.framing: The two gonads are the same machine with different settings. What differs is the output: spermatogenesis makes 4 haploid gametes continuously from a self-renewing stem cell; oogenesis makes 1 from a reservoir that was finished before birth. That single asymmetry explains menopause, polar bodies, and why the two arrest points exist at all.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Map the four cells onto two hormones and you have the lecture: LH → Leydig and theca (androgen); FSH → Sertoli and granulosa (inhibin, and aromatase in the ovary). 4 gametes from spermatogenesis, 1 from oogenesis, and the female reservoir is fixed before birth. The oocyte is arrested twice: prophase I until recruitment, meiosis II until fertilization - fertilization is a trigger, not just a fusion. The blood-testis barrier exists because sperm are genetically foreign to their own host. Most FSH receptors wins the dominant-follicle competition, and assisted reproductive technology simply removes the competition by flooding the system. The granulosa cell trades FSH receptors for LH receptors as ovulation approaches - the same cell, answering to a different hormone. 5-α reductase makes DHT for hair, glands and external genitalia; aromatase makes estradiol and closes the growth plates. Only 5% of testosterone is free, and only that 5% works.

blocks.html: 1. Meiosis and the two gonads at a glance

• In both gonads luteinizing hormone (LH) acts on the steroid-making cell (Leydig, theca) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) acts on the nurse cell (Sertoli, granulosa), and in both the nurse cell makes inhibin to brake FSH
  • Meiosis in the oocyte is asymmetric: at telophase I it splits unequally into the oocyte and a polar body (a little cytoplasm, the unneeded chromosomes, cannot be fertilized)

rows: Leydig cell - in the space BETWEEN the seminiferous tubules; makes testosterone
Sertoli (sustentacular) cell - supports and regulates spermatogenesis, forms the blood-testis barrier, carries FSH receptors, produces inhibin and androgen binding protein
Granulosa cell - aromatizes the theca's testosterone into estrogen; produces inhibin
required for puberty, but NOT perpetually required for Sertoli cell function

blocks.html: 2. Seminiferous tubules and the blood-testis barrier

• The seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis, with a combined length in both testes of up to 1600 metres - that is how the surface area for continuous production is achieved
    • spermatogonia sit at the interstitial side · spermatozoa end up in the lumen
  • The blood-testis barrier
    • prevents immune attack on new sperm - meiosis gives them different genetic material from the host, so without the barrier the person would be infertile
    • prevents passage of cytotoxic agents into the seminiferous tubules
    • establishes an osmotic gradient, which moves fluid into the tubule

blocks.alt: seminiferous tubule - spermatocytes sertoli and leydig cells.png
blocks.cap: Seminiferous tubule in cross section: spermatocytes and Sertoli cells inside the tubule, Leydig cells in the space between tubules

blocks.html: 3. Spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis

rows: spermatogonia replace themselves AND make a primary spermatocyte by MITOSIS → meiotic division → early spermatids
late spermatids lose cytoplasm (discarded as residual bodies) → flagellum develops → acrosome forms on the head, which is what breaks through the cumulus-oocyte complex

blocks.alt: spermatogenesis and spermiogenesis.png
blocks.cap: Sperm development inside a Sertoli cell: spermatogonium by mitosis, primary and secondary spermatocytes through meiosis I and II, then spermatids maturing into spermatozoa (spermiogenesis); notice the tight junction of the blood-testis barrier

blocks.html: 4. Testosterone

• Storage: NOT stored - synthesized in the testis and diffuses straight down its gradient into blood
  • Binding: 95% protein bound - ~50% albumin, 45% sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG)
    • the free 5% is the biologically active fraction
    • why bind it: solubilizes the hydrophobic steroid · protects from catabolism and excretion · acts as storage
  • Rhythm: gonadotropin-releasing hormone, LH and testosterone cycle over ~6 weeks, but far less dramatically than the menstrual cycle
  • Inactivation: liver adds organic acids to the steroid ring (more water soluble) → filtered and excreted by the kidney

rows: DHT is 10× more potent, with receptors in hair follicles, accessory sex glands, and external genitalia
in the central nervous system and adipose tissue. Once estradiol reaches adult levels in males, long bones stop growing

blocks.alt: testosterone conversion to dht and estradiol and their target tissues - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Testosterone and its two conversions: 5-alpha reductase to dihydrotestosterone, aromatase to estradiol, each with its receptor and target tissues

blocks.html: 5. Ovarian function: the reservoir and oogenesis

• The reservoir: oocytes form during embryogenesis, so the oocyte you came from was made while your mother was inside your grandmother (about 5 months' gestation)
    • 1–2 million at birth, down to 300,000 by puberty

rows: begins during gestation; dormant until puberty, and possibly for 50–55 years
FERTILIZATION, which resumes meiosis II and makes a second polar body

blocks.html: 6. Folliculogenesis, ovulation and the corpus luteum

rows: immature and dormant, what is present at birth. At puberty, monthly ovarian factors recruit 30–50 into primary follicles
three features: a DOUBLE layer of theca cells outside, a fluid-filled ANTRUM, and a thickened granulosa layer over the oocyte and lining the antrum
takes 6–8 months to get here; fully developed, secreting hormones, ready to ovulate

blocks.html:
• The follicle with the MOST FSH receptors becomes the dominant follicle, because there is only so much FSH to go around
    • assisted reproductive technology defeats exactly this: injecting supraphysiological FSH overrides dominant-follicle selection, so several follicles get enough FSH and multiple mature at once for harvest
  • Near ovulation the granulosa cell switches receptors: it begins expressing LH receptors and loses its FSH receptors
  • After ovulation, both granulosa and theca cells convert into corpus luteum cells expressing LH receptors, and LH then drives progesterone production
    • implantation succeeds → the corpus luteum is "rescued" · if not → a corpus albicans, a scar, and they accumulate with each ovulation
  • Oocyte-granulosa cell communication is essential, by paracrine signalling and gap-junctional exchange of small regulatory molecules
  • Cyclic changes in the ovary can be read off the histology of the endometrium · ⚠ menstruation itself is limited to humans and some primates
7. What the sex steroids do

rows: muscle: anabolism, builds it · bone: chondrocyte proliferation in the epiphyseal plate, then its closure · skin: activates sebaceous glands
alters body hair distribution (which is why ↓ testosterone causes baldness) · broadens shoulders · relaxes the larynx, deepening the voice · behavioural change

required for differentiation of the epididymis, vas deferens, prostate, seminal vesicles, penis, scrotum · maintains the epididymis, and the function of the seminal vesicles and prostate, which supply fructose, salts and peptides · absolutely required for spermatogenesis

bone: accelerates linear growth AND closes the epiphyseal plates; in adults supports osteoblast and osteocyte activity and prevents resorption · liver: stimulates hepatic protein synthesis, especially SHBG, cortisol-binding globulin and thyroid-binding globulin
fat deposition · growth of the DUCT systems of the breast
stimulates ovulation, regulates the cycle, and acts on the uterine tubes, uterus, cervix and vagina
raises body temperature - mechanism unclear, possibly by interacting with thyroid hormones
develops the LOBULES and ALVEOLI of the mammary glands
with estradiol, acts on the endometrium

blocks.html:
• Breast development splits cleanly between the two hormones: estrogen builds the DUCTS · progesterone builds the LOBULES and ALVEOLI
  • Estrogen does both things to bone: it drives the growth spurt and then ends it by closing the plates - which is also why aromatized oestrogen stops long bone growth in males

lectures.name: Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease
lectures.title: Adrenal Gland Disease
lectures.framing: Every adrenal problem is one zone making too much, or the whole cortex making too little — and each product has exactly one screening test, which is what turns the incidentaloma workup into a fixed list of three.
lectures.keypoints: four products, four screening tests — and an incidentaloma gets three of them. Weight gain is the weakest Cushing sign; bruising, fracture and proximal weakness the strongest. Cushing needs two positive screens before the ACTH question is asked at all. ⭐ Primary insufficiency loses aldosterone as well as cortisol — so K⁺ is high, ACTH is high, and fludrocortisone is required; secondary spares all three. Alpha before beta, always. Cut-offs vary between labs: know the principle, not the number. Gold standards: adrenal vein sampling for lateralising Conn, insulin tolerance test for secondary insufficiency.

blocks.html: 1. The adrenal gland and its axis

• Zones and products: glomerulosa → aldosterone · fasciculata → cortisol · reticularis → androgens · medulla → catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine)
  • Cortisol peaks in the early morning, nadir at night — why the morning (AM) cortisol is the test, and ⚠ a random cortisol is uninterpretable
  • History, always: ask about exogenous steroid use

blocks.alt: adrenal gland regions and hormones released.png
blocks.cap: Adrenal zones and their products: glomerulosa makes aldosterone, fasciculata cortisol, reticularis androgens, and the medulla epinephrine and norepinephrine

blocks.html: 2. Adrenal insufficiency

• Presents as: the symptoms in the table · also recurrent infection
    • physical exam: blood pressure (BP) supine and standing · pigmentation (primary only)
  • Epidemiology: female predominance · primary peaks at 30-50 y (93-140 per million) · secondary peaks at 50-59 y and is the more prevalent (150-280 per million, often exogenous steroid)

rows:
Autoimmune 80-90% in the West
Tuberculosis, fungal, metastases, haemorrhage, drugs
congenital adrenal hyperplasia, adrenoleukodystrophy

Cortex destroyed → both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid lost
Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) ↑ drives pigmentation

Cortex intact but unstimulated
Aldosterone axis preserved

1. AM cortisol 6-9 am — <80 rules in, >450 rules out
2. Paired ACTH — HIGH
3. Electrolytes: Na↓ K↑ HCO₃↓ pH↓ Ca↑, renal insufficiency, eosinophilia
4. Cosyntropin stimulation — the confirmatory test; a rise over 450 is normal, 97% sensitivity and 95% specificity for primary
5. Aldosterone ↓, renin ↑; adrenal antibodies and CT for the cause
⚠ Stop estrogen ≥6 weeks before testing

1. AM cortisol low with ACTH low or inappropriately normal
2. K⁺ normal (sometimes ↑), Na normal or ↓, HCO₃ ↓, aldosterone ↑ as the slide prints it
3. Cosyntropin less reliable here — insulin tolerance test is the gold standard, or corticotropin-releasing hormone
4. MRI pituitary and screen the other anterior axes
5. Ask about exogenous steroid, the commonest cause

Crisis: saline + hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous (IV), do not await results
Chronic: hydrocortisone 10-20 mg AM / 5-10 mg PM (or prednisone 5-7.5 mg AM) plus fludrocortisone
Fatal if missed; lifelong replacement with stress dosing

blocks.html:
• Investigations: AM cortisol 6-9 am with a paired ACTH · cortisol 80-450 → ACTH stimulation test
  • Treatment
    • crisis: 2-3 L saline/dextrose + hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus, then 50-100 mg every 6-8 hours — do not wait for results.
    • chronic: hydrocortisone 10-20 mg AM + 5-10 mg PM (or prednisone 5-7.5 mg AM), plus fludrocortisone 0.05-0.1 mg (often unnecessary in secondary)
    • over-replacement shows as weight gain, hyperglycaemia, hypertension, osteopenia
  • Follow-up: educate every steroid-replaced patient on stress dosing

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • Stress dosing — rule of 3s: flu etc. → 3× the dose for 3 days; surgery → hydrocortisone 50–100 mg 1 h before, then 50–100 mg every 6–8 hours; injection if vomiting

blocks.cap: Step 1 confirms low cortisol (AM cortisol under 80 rules in, over 450 rules out, in between goes to the ACTH stimulation test); step 2 finds the level from ACTH and aldosterone

blocks.html: 3. Cushing syndrome — cortisol ↑

• Causes
    • ACTH-dependent: pituitary, ectopic ACTH or corticotropin-releasing hormone
    • ACTH-independent: adenoma, hyperplasia, carcinoma
    • exogenous steroid is commonest overall
  • Pathology: loss of diurnal rhythm · loss of suppressibility · ↓ feedback sensitivity
  • Presents as: ecchymoses · fragility fracture · proximal muscle weakness · purple striae >1 cm · plethora · hirsutism · glucose intolerance, menstrual irregularity · weight gain, central adiposity
    • physical exam: ecchymoses, thin skin, purple striae >1 cm · proximal weakness — stand from a chair, arms folded · central adiposity, plethora
  • Signs by likelihood ratio — ecchymoses 10-11.3 · osteopenia or fracture 8-13.8 · proximal muscle weakness 8-12.6 · hypertension 4.35-5.29 · edema 2.82-3.88 · purple striae >1 cm 2.72-2.91 · plethora 2.51-3.03 · hirsutism 2.21-2.90 · general obesity 1.75-3.10 · headache 1.27-1.57
  • Investigations
    • Screen — TWO positive tests are required to diagnose from: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone · 24-h urine free cortisol · late-night salivary cortisol
      • positive if: 8-9 am cortisol >50 nmol/L after 1 mg dexamethasone · 24-h urine above the upper limit of normal · late-night saliva >4 nmol/L
    • then ACTH: high = dependent (pituitary, ectopic ACTH or corticotropin-releasing hormone) · low = independent (adrenal adenoma, hyperplasia, carcinoma)
    • localise: MRI pituitary, CT adrenal, or CT chest/abdomen for ectopic ACTH
    • 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test is not useful on an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive pill → use 24-h urine free cortisol
  • Treatment: resect the culprit tumour
  • Prognosis: in remission, not cured — recurrence possible even after 10 years; monitor clinically, 24-h urine and late-night salivary cortisol

blocks.alt: causes of cushing syndrome - pituitary ectopic adrenal exogenous.png
blocks.cap: Causes of Cushing syndrome: ACTH from a pituitary adenoma or lung tumour, adrenal adenoma or carcinoma, or exogenous cortisol

blocks.html: 4. Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn) — aldosterone ↑

• Causes: unilateral adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia · 5-10% of all hypertension · ~1% of incidentalomas
  • Pathology: aldosterone no longer renin-dependent → Na retention, K and H secretion
  • Presents as: resistant hypertension on >3 drugs · low K⁺ — often, not always · no edema
  • Investigations
    • 1. BP and electrolytes — low K⁺, spontaneous or thiazide-induced
    • 2. Screen: plasma aldosterone/renin ratio
    • 3. Confirm non-suppressibility — saline infusion, fludrocortisone, or high-salt
    • 4. Localise — CT abdomen with or without adrenal vein sampling, the gold standard for lateralisation
  • Treatment: unilateral adrenalectomy if one-sided · mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist if bilateral
  • Prognosis: curable if unilateral
5. Pheochromocytoma — catecholamines ↑

• Causes: adrenal medulla, or sympathetic ganglia (paraganglioma) · 1/100,000/yr, <0.2% of hypertension · ~5% of incidentalomas
  • Pathology: catecholamine-secreting tumour
    • 30-40% familial — multiple endocrine neoplasia 2A/2B, von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, succinate dehydrogenase
    • 10% extra-adrenal · 10% bilateral
  • Presents as: spells: headache, palpitations, sweating with pallor · sustained hypertension, anxiety, cold hands, orthostatic drop
  • Investigations
    • Screen: fractionated plasma free metanephrines — 99% sensitivity, 89% specificity, the best single test
    • alternatives: urinary fractionated metanephrines 97% · urinary catecholamines 86% · urinary total metanephrines 77% · ⚠ urinary vanillylmandelic acid only 64% — the most specific (95%) but least sensitive (64%)
    • localise: CT abdomen, or ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE positron emission tomography
    • genetic testing is offered to every diagnosed patient
  • Treatment: alpha blockade BEFORE beta — phenoxybenzamine, then propranolol — then surgery
  • Prognosis: Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal gland Scaled Score <4 benign, >4 aggressive · unrecognised → hypertensive crisis, myocardial infarction
6. Which test for which product, and the incidentaloma

• One screening test per product: aldosterone/renin ratio (aldosterone) · 1 mg overnight dexamethasone, 24-h urine free cortisol, late-night salivary (cortisol) · fractionated plasma free metanephrines, 99% sensitive (catecholamines) · AM cortisol 6-9am with a paired ACTH (insufficiency)
  • Adrenal incidentaloma — screen all three: cortisol (1 mg overnight dexamethasone, 24-h urine) · aldosterone (BP and K⁺, then aldosterone and renin upon indication) · catecholamines (urine or plasma metanephrines)
    • prevalence rises with age — 2-3% over 50, 7% over 70, uncommon under 30
    • the only absolute criterion for malignancy is distant metastasis
    • Never biopsy until pheochromocytoma is excluded — 14 of 20 biopsied patients had a complication (70% complication rate)

lectures.name: Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease
lectures.title: Pituitary Gland Disease
lectures.framing: Every pituitary lesion is asked in two halves — what the mass is doing, and what the gland is making — and a macroadenoma answers both at once.
lectures.keypoints: mass effect and hormone status are two separate questions. Dopamine inhibits prolactin, so antagonists raise it. IGF-1 screens acromegaly because GH is pulsatile, and the OGTT confirms by failure to suppress. ⭐ The prolactinoma is the one pituitary macroadenoma treated medically first — it shrinks on a tablet, so a visual field defect is not an indication for surgery. Acromegaly does not make you taller. Steroid before thyroxine, always. A normal TSH beside a low free T4 is central hypothyroidism, not reassurance.

blocks.html: 1. Two questions for every pituitary lesion

• History — ask each axis in turn
    • adrenal: fatigue, weight loss, hypoglycaemia, hypotension · thyroid: cold intolerance, constipation · gonadal: loss of libido, decreased shaving, amenorrhoea
    • posterior: diabetes insipidus (now called arginine vasopressin (AVP) deficiency) · (prolactin deficiency)
    • mass effect: headache, blurred vision, diplopia
    • screen for galactorrhoea and for acral change (rings, shoes, gloves)
  • Physical exam — formal visual fields — bitemporal hemianopia · lean body habitus, loss of muscle mass, dry skin, minimal androgenic hair · acromegalic features: frontal bossing, large jaw, gapped teeth, macroglossia, positive Tinel's
