blocks.html: 2. Pituitary masses and mass effect

• Mass effect — bitemporal hemianopia (the chiasm carries the crossing nasal fibres) · diplopia from cranial nerves III/IV/VI · headache · pituitary apoplexy
    • draw the fields; a lesion below the chiasm gives a different pattern
  • Non-functioning macroadenoma
    • commonest pituitary adenoma — gonadotroph origin
    • secretes nothing; symptoms are purely mass effect: visual field loss, diplopia, headache, hypopituitarism
    • Investigations: MRI pituitary — the definitive test · formal visual fields · screen every anterior axis for compression — insufficiency is the only hormonal finding
    • Treatment: transsphenoidal surgery · recurrence needs surveillance imaging
  • Follow-up: repeat fields and MRI to confirm the mass has shrunk

blocks.alt: bitemporal hemianopia.png
blocks.cap: Bitemporal hemianopia: a mass pressing on the optic chiasm cuts the crossing nasal fibres from each eye, so both outer (temporal) half-fields are lost

blocks.html: 3. Pituitary insufficiency (hypopituitarism)

• Causes: mass, surgery, radiation, infiltration, infarction, empty sella · hypothalamic: trauma, infection
  • Pathology: compression of the normal gland beside the lesion
  • Presents as: axis by axis: fatigue and hypotension · cold intolerance · ↓libido, ↓shaving · ↑fat, ↓lean mass
  • Investigations
    • 8-9 AM fasting panel, all axes at once: cortisol · TSH AND free T4 — ⚠ free T4, never TSH alone · LH, FSH + testosterone or estradiol · prolactin · GH and IGF-1
    • cortisol <80-100 rules in, >450 rules out; in between needs a stimulation test
    • ⚠ stimulation for cortisol and GH only — the insulin tolerance test is the gold standard (glucose <2.4), with ACTH, corticotropin-releasing hormone and glucagon as alternatives
    • then MRI pituitary for the cause
  • Why a normal TSH does not reassure
    • ⚠ TSH alone is unreliable in secondary hypothyroidism — an "inappropriately normal" TSH beside a low free T4 IS the diagnosis.
    • TSH is an excellent screen for primary thyroid disease and unreliable for secondary
    • the deck's case: TSH 4.11 (range 0.27-4.2) beside a free T4 of 5 (range 10-24) — inappropriately normal
    • free T4 also needs conversion to free triiodothyronine, which needs TSH
  • Treatment
    • replace: hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, testosterone or estradiol; GH is a delayed decision.
    • ⚠ Treat adrenal insufficiency BEFORE hypothyroidism.
  • Follow-up: titrate thyroid replacement on free T4, never TSH · lifelong replacement · stress-dose education for anyone on hydrocortisone

blocks.alt: primary vs secondary hypothyroidism - TRH TSH T4 pattern.png
blocks.cap: Primary vs secondary hypothyroidism: TSH rises in primary but is low or normal in secondary

blocks.html: 4. Overproduction: Cushing disease (ACTH)

• Cause: corticotroph adenoma · ACTH excess → bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
  • Presents as: ecchymoses, fragility fracture, proximal weakness, purple striae
  • Investigations
    • TWO positive screens — dexamethasone, 24-h urine cortisol, late-night salivary
    • ACTH — suppressed = independent (adrenal); normal or ↑ = dependent; ectopic ACTH usually higher than Cushing disease, with overlap
    • 1 mg dexamethasone: traditional cut-off 100 nmol/L (sensitivity 98%, specificity 89%), now 50 nmol/L · 24-h urine >4× upper limit of normal = Cushing, 1-4× = Cushing or pseudo-Cushing
    • MRI pituitary — Cushing disease is a microadenoma in 80-90%, and 40% show nothing on CT or MRI; inferior petrosal sinus sampling is the gold standard when imaging is equivocal
  • Treatment: transsphenoidal surgery (ketoconazole to lower cortisol while waiting) · steroids after surgery to avoid adrenal crisis · remission, not cure
  • Prognosis: untreated 5-year survival <50% (cardiovascular, thromboembolism, infection) · 20% recur after successful surgery (about 1%/yr)
5. Overproduction: prolactinoma

• Cause: lactotroph adenoma
    • also raise prolactin: stalk section, dopamine antagonists, primary hypothyroidism, renal failure, pregnancy
  • Pathology: dopamine normally INHIBITS prolactin — lose the brake and it rises
    • in women 95% microadenomas; macroadenomas commoner in men
  • Presents as
    • women: oligo/amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea 30-70%, infertility
    • men: ↓libido, erectile dysfunction, osteopenia in 80%
    • >100 µg/L = overt hypogonadism
  • Investigations
    • 1. Serum prolactin — normal <25 µg/L, <15 in men
    • 2. Exclude pregnancy, dopamine antagonists, primary hypothyroidism, renal failure, cirrhosis, macroprolactin
    • 3. MRI pituitary — the definitive test
    • 4. assess the mass effect — formal visual fields
    • 5. screen for compression of the other axes
  • Treatment: dopamine agonist FIRST — cabergoline, bromocriptine · surgery is not first option, even with a field defect
  • Prognosis: tumour shrinks on the drug and the field defect lifts; gonadal recovery lags

blocks.html:
• Lactotroph hyperplasia / ↑ prolactin also in pregnancy, estrogen treatment, primary hypothyroidism, and some Cushing's disease
  • Prolactin > 200 ng/mL = lactotroph macroadenoma (pregnancy can just reach it); microadenoma, drugs, stalk and other pituitary disease stay below

blocks.html: 6. Overproduction: acromegaly (GH)

• Cause: GH-secreting adenoma · persistent GH hypersecretion → IGF-1 from the liver drives acral growth
  • Presents as: enlarging hands and feet, coarse features, frontal bossing, gapped teeth, macroglossia, carpal tunnel
    • obstructive sleep apnoea, hypertension 43%, diabetes mellitus 10-15%, colonic polyps
    • height is NOT increased
  • Investigations
    • 1. IGF-1 screens — GH is pulsatile, so a random GH is useless
    • 2. OGTT is the confirmatory test — 75 g, GH every 30 min × 2 h; failure to suppress below 1 µg/L
    • 3. MRI pituitary to localise
    • 4. complications: glucose, blood pressure, echocardiogram, sleep study, colonoscopy
  • Treatment: transsphenoidal surgery · then somatostatin analogue, pegvisomant, radiotherapy
  • Prognosis: mean 12-year diagnostic delay · standardised mortality ratio 1.72 untreated

lectures.name: Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty
lectures.title: Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty
lectures.framing: Puberty is not switched on — the axis is built before birth, suppressed in infancy, and then DISINHIBITED. The menstrual cycle that follows runs on one hormone that reverses its own feedback.
lectures.keypoints: puberty is disinhibition, not activation. ⭐ The earliest measurable change is a NOCTURNAL rise in LH — before puberty LH is flat across 24 hours, and only in late puberty is it raised awake as well. Adrenarche is adrenal and separate from gonadarche, which is why pubic hair can appear with no gonadal activity. Most FSH receptors wins the dominant follicle. Ovulation is 36 hours after the surge. The follicular phase varies; the luteal phase does not. Boys end up taller because they start later, not because they grow faster.

blocks.html: 1. Puberty: the words and the order

• The vocabulary is not interchangeable
    • gonadarche (gonads activated by luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)) · adrenarche (adrenal androgens, a separate axis)
    • thelarche (breast, from ovarian estradiol) · pubarche (pubic hair, from adrenal androgen) · menarche · spermarche
  • Sequence in girls: gonadarche → adrenarche → thelarche → growth spurt → menarche, over 4-5 years (this year's slide order; standard teaching puts adrenarche first)
    • abnormal if it occurs <7 y (precocious) or >16 y (delayed)
  • Genetics accounts for 50-75% of the variation in pubertal timing
  • Boys end up taller because they start later, not because they grow faster
  • History: age at each milestone and the order they came in · family history of pubertal timing · nutrition, weight change, exercise load · anosmia
  • Physical exam: Tanner staging of breast AND pubic hair separately (they run on different axes) · height, weight and plotted growth velocity · thyroid, visual fields, dysmorphism
  • ⚠ No investigation at all is needed for a normally timed, normally ordered puberty — reassurance and explanation where timing is normal
  • Follow-up: re-plot growth velocity and re-stage at interval
2. Hormonal control: what lifts the brake

• Before puberty GABA inhibition dominates glutamate (gamma-aminobutyric acid), so gonadotropin-releasing hormone output is low
  • Kisspeptin acting on GPR54 is the primary trigger
    • regulated by KNDy neurons (kisspeptin, neurokinin B, dynorphin)
    • leptin permissive · MKRN3 inhibitory
    • proof: inactivating GPR54 mutations cause failure to progress through puberty and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, confirmed in knockout mice whose only major phenotype was reproductive
  • The earliest measurable change: a nocturnal rise in LH — flat across 24 hours before puberty, raised awake as well only in late puberty
  • Investigations
    • LH and FSH — timing of the draw matters, because the first rise is at night
    • estradiol · bone age, X-ray of the left wrist
    • thyroid-stimulating hormone and prolactin before calling anything idiopathic

blocks.html: 4. Painful, heavy and premenstrual problems

• Dysmenorrhoea: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, because prostaglandins are the first link in the chain
  • Heavy ovulatory bleeding: tranexamic acid — an antifibrinolytic, a synthetic lysine derivative
  • PMS affects 30-40%, PMDD 3-8% — luteal, resolve with menses
    • Cause: largely unknown — an enhanced response to NORMAL fluctuating estrogen and progesterone, with serotonin and GABA influences
    • Treatment: ovulatory suppression (oral contraceptive pill), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, light therapy
5. Menopause

• Menopause = 12 months of amenorrhoea or FSH consistently >30, mean age 53 (as the slide prints it; usually quoted as about 51)
    • timing is set by the number of follicles present at birth, and by genetics (women tend to reach it at the same age as their mothers)

lectures.name: Disorders of Puberty
lectures.title: Disorders of Puberty
lectures.framing: Two numbers place every pubertal disorder: the age it happened, and the luteinizing hormone (LH). Age sets early against late; LH says whether the brain is driving it or something downstream is.
lectures.keypoints: gonadotropins split every hypogonadism — high means the gonad failed, low means the brain did. ⭐ In a virilised boy, bilaterally enlarged testes mean central and small testes mean peripheral, because only LH grows the testis. Turner is short with streak ovaries; Klinefelter is tall with dysgenic tubules. Kallmann is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism plus anosmia. A single random LH is pulsatile and insensitive — the GnRH stimulation test is the gold standard. Delayed bone age is what makes CDGP the diagnosis.

blocks.html: 1. Normal puberty

• Normal timing — onset 8-13 girls (first sign thelarche), 9-14 boys (first sign testicular volume >3 mL)
    • growth spurt Tanner 2-3 in girls, 3-4 in boys, which is why boys finish taller
    • Menarche ~12.7 y, about 2.5 y after thelarche · girls: breast Tanner 2 at 10.3 y, pubic hair 11.2 y · boys: average onset 11.5 ± 1.3 y
  • Estrogen does: breast development (thelarche) · ↑ growth rate · mood swings · vaginal discharge · menses
  • Androgen does: acne, oily skin and hair, body odour · pubic/axillary hair · penile/clitoral enlargement · voice · ↑ growth rate

blocks.html: 2. Assessing abnormal timing

• History: age at onset of each sign and the ORDER · growth spurt timing · central nervous system (CNS) symptoms — headache, visual change, seizure · head injury, cranial radiation, chemotherapy · medications and any hormone exposure · anosmia · family history: parental heights and parental pubertal timing
  • Physical exam
    • plot height, weight and growth velocity · Tanner stage breast/genital AND pubic hair separately
    • testicular volume by Prader orchidometer — bilaterally ≥4 mL means CENTRAL, virilisation with testes <3 mL means PERIPHERAL · asymmetric testis suggests a Leydig tumour
    • dysmorphism, café-au-lait with irregular "Coast of Maine" borders, neck webbing, cubitus valgus, short 4th metacarpals
  • Investigations: random LH · follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) · estradiol or testosterone · bone age · thyroid-stimulating hormone — then as directed below

lectures.name: Disorders of Growth
lectures.title: Disorders of Growth
lectures.framing: One question splits the differential before any test: did the weight fall before the height, or is the child short and relatively chubby? Illness starves growth; endocrine disease arrests it.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Weight falls first in chronic illness; height falls first in endocrine disease, leaving a short chubby child. Bone age separates familial (on time) from constitutional delay (behind). Disproportionate short stature means skeletal dysplasia, not an endocrine cause. A random GH is worthless because GH is pulsatile. Congenital GH deficiency has a normal birth size and declares itself with neonatal hypoglycaemia.

blocks.html: 1. Measuring height

• Physical exam: accurate height (Frankfurt plane, heels to the board) or length under 2 · weight
    • plot on the right chart — length under 2 on World Health Organization charts, height 2-20 on Centers for Disease Control charts
    • proportionate vs DISPROPORTIONATE (limb vs trunk) · midline defects, micropenis, dysmorphism, goitre, Turner stigmata
  • Triggers to investigate
    • velocity <4.5 cm/yr between age 4 and puberty · crossing percentiles after 18 months
    • >2 standard deviations below mid-parental height · height below the 3rd percentile
2. Evaluating growth: the four questions

• Genetic potential — mid-parental height: (mother + father ± 13)/2, +13 boys, −13 girls
  • Height-age — the age at which this height is the 50th percentile
  • Growth velocity — measurements a full year apart
  • Growth potential — bone age, left wrist, normal ±1 y

blocks.html: 3. Approach to short stature

• History: did the WEIGHT fall before the height, or is the child short and relatively chubby? — that one question splits chronic illness from endocrine disease
    • then: birth weight and length, neonatal hypoglycaemia or prolonged jaundice, diet, gastrointestinal symptoms, chronic illness, cranial radiation, head injury, parental heights and parental pubertal timing
  • Investigations
    • compute mid-parental height and height-age · measure growth velocity over a full year · bone age, left wrist
    • first rule out chronic illness and general causes: complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), renal function (creatinine, urea, electrolytes, albumin, Ca, PO₄), tissue transglutaminase antibodies (celiac), thyroid-stimulating hormone, ferritin
    • then consider: insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) / insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3 · karyotype every short girl · provocative GH test if GH deficiency is suspected
  • Treatment: treat the cause — levothyroxine, withdraw glucocorticoid, gluten-free diet, nutrition
  • Follow-up: re-plot velocity at 6-12 months

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function
lectures.title: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
lectures.framing: Two lines organise the whole lecture: the pelvic pain line, which decides where pain is felt and which block reaches it, and the nodal watershed, which decides where a cancer spreads.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Above the pain line pain refers to flank and back along sympathetics; below it to buttock and thigh along parasympathetics — and that single line predicts both the presentation and the block. Ovarian artery from the aorta, uterine from the internal iliac, and their anastomosis is what lets the ovaries be spared at hysterectomy. Fundus drains para-aortic while cervix drains iliac — one organ, two basins. Clitoris drains to deep inguinal, labial skin to superficial.

blocks.html: 1. The reproductive tract

• Uterus — anteverted (relative to the vagina) and anteflexed (relative to the cervix); rests on the empty bladder
    • body:cervix tracks hormone exposure: neonate 2:1 (maternal hormones) · childhood 1:1 · post-pubertal 2:1 · multiparous 3:1 · postmenopausal 1:1
  • Vagina — between urethra and rectum; posterior fornix is deepest
    • rectouterine pouch is the lowest point when upright
  • Uterine tubes — within the mesosalpinx · fertilization in the AMPULLA, which is also the commonest ectopic site
  • Ovary — never enters the inguinal canal, unlike the testis
  • Physical exam
    • abdominal exam by quadrant · bimanual to size the uterus and assess mobility and adnexae · speculum for the cervix
    • through the thin vaginal wall you can palpate the cervix, ischial spines, sacral promontory, uterine artery pulsation and ovarian irregularity
2. Seeing the tract

• Investigations
    • beta-human chorionic gonadotropin first in any woman of reproductive age
    • pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal)
    • hysterosalpingography (HSG) for tubal patency — contrast should spill into the peritoneum
    • culdocentesis via the posterior fornix for free fluid, since the rectouterine pouch is the lowest point when upright
3. Support and the pelvic floor

• Uterine ligaments
    • cardinal ligament carries the uterine vessels; uterosacral prevents prolapse
    • broad ligament = mesometrium, mesosalpinx, mesovarium
    • ovary: suspensory ligament carries the ovarian vessels · ligament of the ovary anchors it to the uterus
  • Perineal body — central, midway between the ischial tuberosities, the final support of the pelvic viscera
  • Pelvic diaphragm — levator ani (puborectalis medially, pubococcygeus intermediately, iliococcygeus posterolaterally) and coccygeus
  • A transverse line between the ischial tuberosities divides the perineum into the urogenital and anal triangles
4. Blood supply

• Uterus: uterine artery — from the INTERNAL ILIAC, runs in the cardinal ligament
    • "Water under the bridge" — the ureter passes UNDER the uterine artery; identify it at hysterectomy
  • Ovary: ovarian artery — from the AORTA
    • the ovarian collateral (its anastomosis with the uterine) lets the ovaries be spared at hysterectomy
  • Uterine tubes: tubal branches of uterine and ovarian
  • Vagina: vaginal artery (middle) · internal pudendal (inferior)
  • Perineum: internal pudendal — out the greater sciatic foramen, behind the sacrospinous ligament, back in via the lesser

6. Nerves and the pelvic pain line

• Fundus and body ABOVE the pain line — sympathetic to T11/12-L2 (tubes and ovaries too) → pain referred to mid-trunk, back, flank
  • Cervix and vagina BELOW the line — parasympathetic to S2-S4 → pain referred to gluteal region, thigh, leg
  • Perineum: pudendal nerve (S2-S4), felt in the perineum directly · dorsal nerve of the clitoris is the primary sensory nerve
  • History
    • WHERE is the pain referred? Flank, back and mid-trunk point above the line; buttock, thigh and leg point below it
    • then: cycle relationship, dyspareunia (superficial vs deep), bowel and bladder symptoms, obstetric and surgical history, trauma or straddle injury
  • Anaesthesia, chosen by the pain line
    • lumbar epidural or low spinal (L3/4) anaesthetises everything below the waist
    • caudal (saddle) epidural reaches S2-S4 only and does not block the uterine fundus, so the mother still feels contractions and knows when to bear down
    • pudendal block at the ischial spine covers the perineum and inferior quarter of the vagina but does not reach the cervix or superior vagina
    • ⚠ Contractions are hormonal, not neural — no block stops labour

blocks.html: 7. The perineum, its fascia and episiotomy

• Perineal fascia and where fluid goes
    • a ruptured urethra fills the superficial perineal pouch (Colles fascia ↔ perineal membrane)
    • it cannot reach the thigh (Colles binds to the fascia lata) and cannot reach the anal triangle (Colles stops at the urogenital triangle)
    • so it tracks up the anterior abdominal wall, deep to Camper's and Scarpa's but superficial to external oblique
    • the deep pouch holds the voluntary external urethral sphincter, through which both the vagina and urethra pass in the female
  • Physical exam: perineal body integrity, scars, swelling and where it does and does not track
  • Episiotomy — median episiotomy divides the perineal body and directs tearing toward the anus; mediolateral is safer
    • mediolateral over median: the median cut brings more severe laceration, incontinence and fistula

blocks.cap: Perineal pouches in female and male: the deep pouch above the perineal membrane, the superficial pouch below it, bounded by Colles fascia

blocks.html: 8. Erectile tissue and the sexual response

• Homologues: glans clitoris ↔ glans penis · crura of clitoris ↔ crura of penis (corpora cavernosa) · bulbs of vestibule ↔ bulb of penis · labia majora ↔ scrotum (and the round ligament ends in the labia majora) · greater vestibular glands (superficial pouch) ↔ bulbourethral glands (deep pouch)
  • Superficial perineal muscles, all pudendal (S2-S4): ischiocavernosus maintains erection · bulbospongiosus assists erection and in the female supports the perineal body, acts as a vaginal sphincter and compresses the greater vestibular glands · superficial transverse perineal fixes the perineal body
  • Arousal is psychogenic or reflexogenic; erection is parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnics S2-S4 → cavernous nerves → helicine arteries dilate, veins compressed); ejaculation is sympathetic — "point and shoot"
  • Sexual response cycle: desire → arousal (central, non-genital peripheral, genital) → orgasm → resolution
    • limited data exist on the female anatomy and physiology of the sexual response

lectures.name: Development of the Female Reproductive System
lectures.title: Development of the Female Reproductive System
lectures.framing: Female is the default: no testis-determining factor makes the ovary, no anti-Müllerian hormone keeps the Müllerian ducts, no testosterone dissolves the Wolffian ducts. Every anomaly below is one failed step in the fusion-and-canalisation sequence.
lectures.keypoints: Wolffian and Müllerian are reciprocal — one survives in each sex. Didelphys and bicornuate are failed FUSION; septate is failed RESORPTION; unicornuate is one duct that never formed. The vagina has two origins, upper third from the ducts and lower two-thirds from the bulbs. Absent vagina usually means absent uterus. ⭐ Always image the renal tract when a Müllerian anomaly is found — both systems arise from intermediate mesoderm, and urinary development precedes genital by about 10 days.

blocks.html: 1. Sex determination: the default pathway

• SRY gene present → testis-determining factor → testis · absent → ovary
  • No anti-Müllerian hormone → paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts develop · no testosterone → mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts degenerate
  • Wolffian and Müllerian are reciprocal — one survives in each sex.

blocks.html: 2. The indifferent gonad

• Primordial germ cells migrate from the yolk sac (weeks 4-6, ~T10) to the gonadal ridge — no migration, no gonad
  • Sexes are indifferent weeks 4-7 and distinct by week 12
  • By week 7 both duct systems sit side by side
3. The ovary and the oocyte reserve

• Primitive sex cords degenerate, cortical cords form, oogonia become primary oocytes arrested in prophase I
  • ~400,000 at birth, and no oogonia form postnatally — the reserve is fixed before birth
4. Mesonephric (Wolffian) remnants

• All in the broad ligament
    • epoöphoron (mesovarium) · paroöphoron (near the uterus)
    • Gartner's duct (lateral uterine and vaginal wall), which is the one that becomes a cyst
  • A Gartner's duct cyst in the lateral vaginal wall is a mesonephric remnant and needs no workup beyond recognition

blocks.html: 5. Paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts and the vagina's two origins

• Paramesonephric ducts open cranially as the tubes and fimbriae and fuse caudally into the uterovaginal primordium → uterus, cervix, upper 1/3 vagina
  • this induces the sinovaginal bulbs, which fuse into the vaginal plate and canalise into the lower 2/3
  • The vagina has two origins: upper third from the ducts, lower two-thirds from the bulbs
  • The hymen ruptures perinatally

• Didelphys and bicornuate are failed FUSION; septate is failed RESORPTION; unicornuate is one duct that never formed.

blocks.html:
• Absent vagina usually means absent uterus.
  • History: primary amenorrhoea with or without normal secondary sexual characteristics · cyclical pain without bleeding (obstruction) · recurrent miscarriage or preterm delivery (fusion anomaly) · dyspareunia or an inability to use tampons · always ask about known RENAL anomalies
  • Physical exam: external genitalia and whether the structures fused · patency and length of the vagina · presence of a cervix · bimanual for a uterus · Tanner staging (normal breasts with absent uterus points elsewhere than gonadal failure)
  • Investigations: pelvic ultrasound first, then MRI for uterine morphology · karyotype · hormones to confirm ovarian function
    • ⚠ imaging the RENAL tract is mandatory, not optional, whenever a Müllerian anomaly is found — urinary and genital defects travel together, because both arise from intermediate mesoderm
  • Follow-up: counsel that many of these women are fertile but carry an increased rate of premature delivery, so pregnancies are followed as high risk
7. Descent of the ovary

• The gubernaculum tethers the ovary, which descends retroperitoneally but never enters the inguinal canal
  • Its midpoint splits into the ligament of the ovary and the round ligament of the uterus
  • As with the testis, the ovary's innervation, blood supply and lymphatic drainage reflect its posterior abdominal origin
8. External genitalia

• Driven by estrogens and the absence of dihydrotestosterone, weeks 9-14
  • genital tubercle → clitoris, urethral folds → labia minora, labioscrotal swellings → labia majora
  • All three stay separated — female external development is defined by structures not fusing
  • the urogenital membrane breaks down at week 7, exposing the vestibule

lectures.name: Introduction to Transgender Medicine
lectures.title: Introduction to Transgender Medicine
lectures.framing: Four words that are not synonyms, and a treatment ladder ordered by one thing: reversibility.
lectures.keypoints: dysphoria is the distress, not the incongruence. Blockers fully reversible, hormones partially, surgery not — and hormones wait until puberty has started. Fertility is discussed before hormones, not after. Comorbidity must be reasonably well-controlled, not cured. Testosterone effects are not fully reversible, and oral testosterone cannot be monitored at all. ⭐ Family support moves suicide attempt risk from 60% to 4%.

blocks.html: 1. Definitions

• Sex is biological
  • Gender is psychological
  • Gender identity is the person's own articulation
  • Sexual orientation is a separate axis entirely
2. Gender dysphoria

• Diagnosis — gender dysphoria is the DISTRESS, not the incongruence
    • marked and persistent incongruence, a desire to transition and be accepted as the experienced gender
    • a strong dislike of one's sexual anatomy or of anticipated pubertal changes
  • Assessment — summarised as insistence · persistence · consistence (how long, how fixed, how consistent across settings)
    • History: "Some young people feel they were born in the wrong body; have you ever felt like that?" · how puberty affected their identity · source of distress · social transition and who knows · fertility intentions
    • ⚠ family support, which is the single largest modifier of suicide risk (60% → 4%)
    • Physical exam: Tanner stage (it decides whether blockers or hormones are even on the table) · height, weight, blood pressure · baseline for the effects being monitored
  • Epidemiology — 1 in 300 Canadians aged 15+, two-thirds under 35 · 1.2-4.1% of adolescents · prevalence is rising, not falling
    • Most PRE-pubertal children who identify as transgender do not persist; most ADOLESCENTS do — which is why puberty is where the ladder begins
  • Mental health outcomes
    • suicidality is 2-3× more frequent · 47% of trans youth in Ontario had considered suicide, 19% attempted
    • youth managed with hormones, surgery where indicated and a multidisciplinary team including mental health clinicians had outcomes similar to the general population

• puberty blockers (fully reversible) → gender-affirming hormones (partially reversible) → surgery (irreversible)

blocks.html:
• Puberty blockers need Tanner 2 + informed consent (dysphoria long-standing, worse with puberty, co-existing problems addressed)
  • Gender-affirming hormones: usually around age 16, patient able to consent, preferably with parental consent/support — not "any age"
  • Genital surgery only after the age of majority + 1 year living in the gender role; top surgery can be earlier — age 16, after 1 year of hormones

blocks.html: 4. WPATH criteria and guidelines

• Criteria for hormones: persistent documented dysphoria · capacity to consent · age of majority or the adolescent SOC · ⚠ comorbidity "reasonably well-controlled", NOT resolved
  • Fertility preservation is discussed before hormones, not after
  • Guidelines — WPATH Standards of Care v8 (2022) and the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2017)
    • the endocrinologist's role is bounded: initial treatment considerations, advice when issues arise, and explicitly not necessarily diagnostic
5. Hormone therapy and monitoring

• Investigations before hormones: health history, risk assessment and relevant baseline labs
  • Testosterone levels: total testosterone plus SHBG
    • ⚠ SHBG falls in obesity and distorts the total · free androgen index = T/SHBG
    • ⚠ oral testosterone cannot be monitored at all · injected testosterone is measured halfway between doses · transdermal any time
  • Follow-up: ongoing monitoring of effectiveness and side effects, communication with primary care, mental health and surgeon
    • every 3 months in the first year, then 1-2 times a year
    • trans women: testosterone <50 ng/dL, estradiol not above the peak physiological 100-200 pg/mL, potassium if on spironolactone
    • trans men: testosterone 400-700 ng/dL (mid-way between injections) · haematocrit or haemoglobin · weight, blood pressure, lipids
  • Risks (WPATH, likely increased)
    • feminizing: venous thromboembolism, gallstones, raised liver enzymes, weight gain, hypertriglyceridemia · cardiovascular disease with added risk factors · possibly hypertension, hyperprolactinemia or prolactinoma
    • masculinizing: polycythemia, weight gain, acne, androgenic alopecia, sleep apnea · possibly raised liver enzymes, hyperlipidemia
    • the Stein slides attribute the risks to inadvertent or intentional supraphysiological doses
6. Surgery

• Irreversible, the last step · needs 1-2 mental health referrals; Ontario requires two providers
  • Top surgery can come earlier (age 16) than genital surgery (age of majority)

lectures.name: Disorders of Sexual Differentiation
lectures.title: Disorders of Sexual Differentiation
lectures.framing: A disorder of sexual differentiation (DSD) is a discrepancy between karyotype, gonad, internal genitalia and external genitalia — so the karyotype is the first test, because it decides which half of the differential you are in. The lecture builds the normal pathway, examines and investigates the newborn, splits the causes by karyotype, then manages the baby and the commonest cause, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH).
lectures.keypoints: karyotype first. 5α-reductase deficiency virilises at puberty (incompletely) because testosterone is normal; incomplete androgen insensitivity virilises only incompletely and adds gynaecomastia and azoospermia. T:DHT after hCG for the enzyme, DNA for the receptor. DHT builds the external genitalia, testosterone the internal ducts. ⭐ The 46,XX CAH infant looks ambiguous and is caught at birth; the 46,XY CAH infant looks normal and presents in salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks. Sex assignment does not inevitably mean surgery.

blocks.html: 1. How sex develops, and what a DSD is

• Male path: the SRY gene makes testis-determining factor (TDF) → testes
    • Sertoli cells: anti-Mullerian hormone (Mullerian-inhibiting factor, MIF) → the Mullerian duct regresses
    • Leydig cells: testosterone → keeps the Wolffian duct → internal male genitalia
    • 5-alpha-reductase turns testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT) → external male genitalia
  • Female path is the default without SRY — but a 46,XX karyotype is needed for normal ovarian development
  • DHT builds the external genitalia, testosterone the internal ducts

blocks.cap: Sexual differentiation: SRY makes testis-determining factor (TDF) and testes; Sertoli cells make anti-Mullerian hormone (MIF) to regress the Mullerian duct, Leydig testosterone keeps the Wolffian duct, and 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT for male external genitalia; without SRY, the female path is the default

blocks.title: What this lecture is explicitly NOT about
blocks.html: ⚠ Gender identity, gender expression and sexual orientation are stated on their own slide as out of scope. A DSD is an anatomical and biochemical finding. ⚠ DSDs are not always associated with ambiguous genitalia — some present instead as abnormal pubertal development.
2. Examining the newborn

• History
    • family history of ambiguous genitalia, virilisation, infertility or unexplained neonatal death · consanguinity
    • pregnancy: maternal medications, maternal virilisation, maternal health
    • neonatal crisis — vomiting, poor feeding, collapse at 1-3 weeks
  • Physical exam
    • PALPATE FOR GONADS — a palpable gonad is almost always a testis, which immediately narrows the differential
    • phallus length and width · labioscrotal folds: fused or open, rugated, hyperpigmented · number and position of urogenital openings
    • describe it with a drawn diagram, not prose
    • general exam for dysmorphism and for hyperpigmentation (excess adrenocorticotropic hormone, ACTH)
  • Use neutral terms: gonads, phallus, labio-scrotal folds.
3. Investigations: the karyotype splits the differential

• First line, every case: karyotype · pelvic and abdominal ultrasound
  • Then other labs based on your differential
    • 17-hydroxyprogesterone (markedly raised in 21-hydroxylase deficiency) · electrolytes and glucose — sodium↓, potassium↑, acidosis, low blood sugar
    • testosterone:DHT (T:DHT) ratio after human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) stimulation for 5-alpha-reductase deficiency
    • DNA analysis for androgen insensitivity
  • Two further karyotype groups: ovotesticular DSD (chromosomes variable, gonads mixed) · mixed gonadal dysgenesis (45,X/46,XY)

blocks.html: 4. 46,XY DSD: an under-virilised male
Testes are present, but the external genitalia are incompletely virilised.

• Causes
    • testis failed: gonadal dysgenesis (complete or partial) · testes regression
    • cannot make androgen: Leydig cell hypoplasia (luteinizing hormone (LH) deficiency or LH receptor defect) · testosterone biosynthesis defects (non-virilising CAH: 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3β-HSD), 17,20-lyase, 17β-HSD) · deficient anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) synthesis or action
    • cannot make DHT: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency (autosomal recessive)
    • receptor broken: androgen insensitivity (X-linked recessive androgen receptor defect)
5. 46,XX DSD: a virilised female
Ovaries are present, but a source of androgen has virilised the external genitalia.

• Causes
    • CAH from 21-hydroxylase deficiency — the commonest
    • androgen-secreting tumour
    • transplacental maternal androgen or drugs

blocks.html: 6. Managing ambiguous genitalia at birth

• Refer to a tertiary centre — endocrinology, neonatology, genetics, gynaecology, urology, social work, psychology
  • Delay assignment of sex of rearing, do not assign a name, do not register the birth until investigations are complete
  • warn that a final diagnosis may take several weeks
  • Sex assignment does not inevitably mean surgery — evidence for the operations is lacking and only expert surgeons should be involved
7. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)

• Cause: Autosomal recessive, CYP21A2 on chromosome 6; 95% of all CAH is 21-hydroxylase deficiency
  • Pathology: cortisol blocked → ACTH ↑ → adrenal hyperplasia → precursors shunted to androgen; aldosterone lost in 75%
  • Shares of CAH: 21-hydroxylase ≈95% · 11β-hydroxylase 5% · 3β-HSD 1%; incidence 1 in 10,000 births
  • Severity is set by residual enzyme activity
    • <1% = salt wasting (75% of 21-hydroxylase deficiency), crisis at 1-3 weeks, fatal if missed
    • 1-5% = simple virilising: cortisol deficiency and androgen excess without significant salt loss
    • mild mutation = non-classic: premature pubarche, then hirsutism, acne and oligomenorrhoea — a polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome-like picture
  • Presents as
    • Girls: virilised — clitoral hypertrophy, labial fusion, single urogenital opening · Boys: LOOK NORMAL — penile enlargement, scrotal pigmentation
    • salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks
  • Investigations: 17-hydroxyprogesterone markedly raised — the diagnostic marker (case: 400, normal <10) · sodium↓ potassium↑, acidosis, low blood sugar
  • Treatment
    • lifelong hydrocortisone 10-15 mg/m²/day divided, plus fludrocortisone 0.05-0.20 mg · extra oral saline in infants
    • stress dosing during illness to prevent a salt-losing crisis
  • Acute salt-losing crisis (review session, case: sodium 110, potassium 8.4, glucose 2.5, 17-hydroxyprogesterone 1365)
    • fluids: 5% dextrose/normal saline (D5/NS), no potassium, resuscitate at 20 ml/kg, then 1.5-2 × maintenance
    • IV hydrocortisone bolus 2 mg/kg, then infusion 100 mg/m²/day
    • fludrocortisone 0.1-0.3 mg/day

lectures.name: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS)
lectures.title: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS)
lectures.framing: Renamed from polycystic ovary syndrome in 2026 because both halves of the old name were wrong. The diagnosis is a triad that needs no ultrasound, made by excluding the mimics of each limb separately — hyperandrogenism has its own list of them, ovulatory dysfunction has another. The lecture then works each limb (history, exam, labs), the insulin resistance behind the risk, the myths, and treatment.
lectures.keypoints: the follicles are arrested antral follicles and the ovary is a target, not the source — which is why the name changed. ⭐ Hyperandrogenism plus oligomenorrhoea plus clean exclusions is diagnostic without ever scanning her; ultrasound is an alternative route into the second limb, not a criterion of its own. Cystic ovaries are also not specific — they occur early after menarche and in normally cycling women, so the scan is neither required for the diagnosis nor sufficient for it. Testosterone only reads against its two ranges — female normal < 2 nmol/L, male from ~8 — so 2.1-2.5 is fractionally over and fits, while 10 is a male level and means a tumour; and a normal testosterone does not exclude PMOS, because clinical hyperandrogenism satisfies that limb by itself. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is what separates non-classic CAH from PMOS when the picture is otherwise identical. Acanthosis is the insulin sign; striae would mean Cushing's. Hirsutism is defined by distress, not by a score — the modified Ferriman-Gallwey grades it but ignores ethnicity and hair removal. Of the five treatments offered, only topical testosterone is wrong. Reassure that she can conceive — and advise contraception in the same breath.

blocks.html: 1. The name, and what PMOS is

• Old name, two errors
    • "polycystic": the follicles are arrested antral follicles, not cysts
    • "ovary syndrome": the ovary is a target, not the source
  • How common: over 170 million women, up to 20% of reproductive age
  • Cause: multisystem; no single cause identified
    • hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian dysregulation · luteinizing hormone↑ follicle-stimulating hormone↓
    • insulin resistance
    • adipose converts adrenal androgen to testosterone

blocks.alt: pcos pathophysiology - insulin resistance, shbg, lh and hyperandrogenism - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: PCOS pathophysiology: insulin resistance lowers sex hormone-binding globulin and raises free estradiol and LH, driving ovarian hyperandrogenism, while raised P450c17 activity adds ovarian and adrenal androgen

blocks.html: 2. Diagnosis: the triad

• All three needed
    • ① hyperandrogenism — on exam or on labs
    • ② ovulatory dysfunction — oligomenorrhoea or cystic ovaries on ultrasound
    • ③ exclusion of other disorders
  • There is no gold-standard test — the diagnosis IS the clinical triad, and no ultrasound is required
3. Excluding the mimics

• First-line panel: 1. Exclusion panel first: beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) · prolactin · thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) · total testosterone
    • beta-hCG → pregnancy · prolactin (normal < 20 nmol/L) → prolactinoma · TSH, with free thyroxine (T4) if it is suppressed → thyroid disease
  • The lecture's own exclusion list is seven — pregnancy · hyperprolactinaemia · exogenous testosterone · tumour producing testosterone · congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) · hyperthyroidism · early menarche or menopause
  • Three of the seven are found by history, not by a disease work-up (so they have no column below)
    • exogenous androgen: taking testosterone, or skin contact with a partner's topical testosterone — found only on a thorough medication and social history
    • pregnancy: suspected on history, settled by beta-hCG
    • early menarche or menopause: a thorough menstrual history, and no test beyond it
  • Rate of onset is the other history discriminator: PMOS hirsutism creeps over years, a tumour's arrives fast
  • Cushing syndrome keeps a column here but is not on the list of seven: the deck names adrenal Cushing's only as a source of an androgen-secreting tumour, while the lecture's case still argues against Cushing's explicitly, on absent striae and a normal fasting glucose

blocks.html: 4. Hyperandrogenism: history and exam

• History
    • hirsutism: location, timing of onset and rate of onset · family history of hirsutism
    • acne: location and timing · alopecia: presence and timing
    • rate of onset, ethnicity and parental appearance must all be weighed before calling hair growth abnormal
    • a rapid onset is the tumour question, not a PMOS one
  • Exam
    • terminal hair in a male pattern (face, chin, chest, upper arms) · acne · frontal alopecia
    • score the hair with the modified Ferriman-Gallwey system — 9 sites, each graded 1-4
  • Hirsutism is defined by distress, not by a score — the modified Ferriman-Gallwey grades it but ignores ethnicity and hair removal

blocks.cap: Modified Ferriman-Gallwey score: nine body sites, each graded 1 to 4 for terminal hair; it grades hirsutism, but distress defines it

blocks.html: 5. Hyperandrogenism: labs

• Total testosterone, read against both ranges: normal female is < 2 nmol/L, the male range starts ~8 nmol/L
    • 2.1-2.5 nmol/L is fractionally over the female ceiling and fits PMOS
    • 10 nmol/L is inside the male range and suggests an androgen-secreting tumour
  • A normal testosterone does not exclude PMOS — clinical hyperandrogenism satisfies the limb on its own
  • 17-hydroxyprogesterone where non-classic CAH is in question
6. Oligomenorrhoea: history

• age at menarche and how often periods came initially, in the later teens, and after age 20
  • oral contraceptive use · family history of irregular menses and infertility
  • galactorrhoea, whose absence is what removes the prolactinoma
  • If menses became irregular on stopping an oral contraceptive pill, the pill did not cause it — it masked oligomenorrhoea she already had
7. Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound

• The peripheral follicles are arrested antral follicles, not true cysts
  • Pelvic ultrasound is NOT required — hyperandrogenism plus oligomenorrhoea plus clean exclusions is already diagnostic
  • Cystic ovaries are not specific — they occur early after menarche and in normally cycling women

blocks.html: 8. Insulin resistance: history, body habitus and skin

• History
    • a gentle weight history — did the cycle become irregular after significant weight gain
    • personal history of prediabetes, obstructive sleep apnoea or metabolic liver disease
    • family history of gestational diabetes and type 2 diabetes · mood · medications · fertility intentions and current contraception
  • Exam
    • blood pressure, BMI, and central adipose distribution — visual assessment can suffice, or waist ÷ hip, over 0.85 in women
    • acanthosis nigricans over the back of the neck and in the axilla, with skin tags beside it — the insulin-resistance signs
    • striae are NOT expected — violaceous striae point at Cushing's instead
  • Labs: metabolic screening — fasting glucose or A1c, lipid panel
9. Myths the module asks you to dispel

• TRUE: subfertility and early miscarriage · metabolic syndrome correlates · endometrial cancer · mood disorders
  • FALSE: cannot lose weight · constantly hungry · organic or vegan diet helps · cannot conceive
  • Every false one blames the patient; every true one is a real clinical risk. Counsel with "no body shaming" and meet patients where they are
10. Associated conditions

• More common in PMOS: endometrial carcinoma · gestational diabetes · central adipose distribution · frontal alopecia
  • Adrenal hypertrophy is not
11. Treatment and managing risk

• Treat the symptom of distress
    • oligomenorrhoea: BCP or cyclical progesterone
    • subfertility: lifestyle · aromatase inhibitors to induce ovulation · surgical reduction of ovarian stromal mass (partial resection, drilling, thermal ablation — rare now) · metformin arguably for early miscarriage
    • hirsutism: surface therapies (epilation, shaving, sugaring, waxing, laser) · antiandrogens (spironolactone, cyproterone) · birth control pill · topical eflornithine
    • alopecia: minoxidil 5% · antiandrogens · birth control pill · hair transplant
    • only topical testosterone is the wrong answer
  • Lifestyle throughout: high fibre, low fat, ~30 min planned exercise daily, modest weight loss — "no body shaming"
  • Managing risk
    • metabolic: monitor for DM, HTN and cardiovascular disease · 150 minutes planned vigorous exercise weekly, high-fibre low-fat diet, modest weight loss · consider bariatric surgery, "quite effective for restoring menstrual cycles and fertility"
    • Endometrial carcinoma: induce withdrawal bleeds at least 4× a year with an oral contraceptive or cyclical progesterone, plus ultrasound surveillance for hypertrophy
  • Counsel that she can conceive spontaneously, so contraception is still needed
